 Recovery testing procedures
 Perceptual measures. A 5-item questionnaire from McLean et al. [21] to rate sleep qual-
 ity, fatigue, muscle soreness, stress and mood on a 5-point Likert scale was used. Overall well-
 ness was assessed by summing the 5 scores. Reliability of the questionnaire has been assessed
 in a previous study and showed a coefficient of variation of 7.1% (5.8% to 9.1%) [22].
 Cognitive function. A Stroop test was used to assess cognitive function as it involves
 brain areas such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex and the anterior cingulate cortex [23]
 which have been shown to be influenced by sleep loss [24]. The test was performed on Ence-
 phalApp (EncephalApp, HindSoft Technology, India) and performed on an electronic tablet
 (Ipad, Apple, USA). Recent literature review reporting the test-retest reliability of a computer-
 ized Stroop task highlighted good level of reliability (ICC>0.90) [25]. Participants performed
 one set comprising 10 repetitions. Participants were required to answer appropriately to a
 series of colour words under conditions where word meanings and ink colours are incongru-
 ent (e.g. the word green displayed in red ink) or congruent (e.g. the word red printed in red
 ink). Before each session, two practice tests were performed to avoid any learning effects. For
 each session, participants completed the testing in an isolated room to avoid any disturbances.
 Each participant was asked to be seated and perform the test with the same hand throughout
 the study. The time to complete the task was used for analysis.
 Autonomic function. Players completed 5 min of running 20 m shuttles at a submaximal
 running speed fixed at 9 km�h-1, followed immediately by 2 min of passive recovery during
 which heart rate recovery (HRR) was determined as described by Buchheit et al. [26]. Post-

 [26]. Recent investigation showed a coefficient of variation of 3.4% among similar rugby league
 players [27].
 Locomotor efficiency. Following the sub-maximal running test, participants performed
 four paced, high speed runs to allow for the calculation of running load index (RLI) as a mea-
 sure of locomotor efficiency as per previous methods [28]. Each run was 60 m and players
 were paced to complete the run in 12 seconds (mean velocity � 18 km�h-1). This method has
 demonstrated a large relationship with leg stiffness (r = 0.62) as well as a small typical error (=
 0.54) [28].
 Neuromuscular function. Countermovement jump (CMJ) and plyometric push-up (PP)
 were performed on a force plate (PASPORT force plate, PS-2141, PASCO Scientific, Califor-
 nia, USA). CMJ mean power and PP flight-time were used for analysis as they have been
 deemed as reliable markers of fatigue in rugby union [22].
 Statistical analysis
 All data were log transformed to reduce bias as a result of nonuniformity error. Data were ana-
 lysed using linear mixed models within R Studio (Version 1.1.442, R Foundation for Statistical
 Computing). Time course of recovery within group were assessed by running two separate
 models and considering period of assessment (POST 0, POST 14, POST 36) as the fixed effect
 and pre training session (PRE) testing battery as reference for comparison. Regarding the
 effect of conditions (SE vs. CON), between groups comparisons were performed using the
 condition as fixed effect. In all models, participants were considered as a random factor. Dif-
 ferences were assessed with the least square means test and further with standardized effect
 sizes (ES) and 90% confidence interval (CI) derived from mixed model analysis. Further com-
 parisons were then performed with a magnitude-based decision framework (MBD) [29]. The
 ES magnitude was classified as trivial (<0.2), small (0.2–0.6), moderate (>0.6–1.2), large
 (>1.2–2.0) and very large (>2.0–4.0) (Hopkins, 2009). The effects were considered practically
 meaningful if the likelihood of a true effect was > 75%.

459	 interventions are in themselves acute, and that recovery interventions will have varied effects
460	 on the diverse aspects of recovery during this acute period. Consequently, if athletes must per-
461	 form again within short timeframes (e.g. multi days event, congested fixtures), practitioners
462	 can consider which recovery protocols that best align to the performance requirements. In
463	 cases where longer recovery is possible, it remains unknown if a sleep extension performed
464	 over several days would be more beneficial than active recovery.
465	 Standardized training session and acute responses
466	 The results of the current study suggest that the standardised training session induced imme-
467	 diate (i.e. POST 0) and substantial changes in perceptual fatigue measures, neuromuscular
468	 function and HRR. Neither cognitive nor upper body neuromuscular parameters were affected
469	 by the training exposure at POST 0. The decreases in perceptual fatigue and lower body neuro-
470	 muscular function were persistent at POST 14 and POST 36. Roe et al. [16] reported similar
471	 results regarding perceptual recovery despite different responses regarding the neuromuscular
472	 function. While Roe et al. [16] observed a change in upper body neuromuscular function, in
473	 the present study, only lower body neuromuscular function was affected. The reason for this
474	 difference remains hypothetical but could be related to the player level (academy vs. univer-
475	 sity). No between group differences were observed at POST 0 for any measure indicating that
476	 the training exposure caused similar fatigue effects in both conditions. Collectively, these
477	 results suggest that the standardized training session is a reliable protocol to induce substantial
478	 fatigue responses over two days and could be used for future research.
479	 The effects of sleep extension and active recovery on sleep parameters at
480	 night 1
481	 During night 1, the SE intervention elicited a very large increase in the time spent in bed and
482	 consequently total sleep time in comparison to CON. However, while time in bed improved,
483	 total sleep time only demonstrated a small improvement compared to baseline (� 1 hour)
484	 reaching only the 7h of total sleep time which is line with recommendation for healthy individ-
485	 ual [30] but potentially below what is recommended and needed for athletes [31, 32]. In a simi-
486	 lar study [9], participants increased total sleep time only by 1h after a football match played in
487	 the evening (i.e. match finished at 22:30). These results suggest that it is difficult to acutely
488	 extend total sleep time by more than 1h in team sport athletes. This may be because the rapid
489	 change in sleep schedule conflicts with established circadian rhythms [33]. While in this study,
490	 participants slept in their home environment, in practical settings, elite athletes often slept in
491	 different environment could also limits the integration of sleep extension for this population.
492	 Furthermore, poorer sleep on Night 2 (i.e. shorter total sleep time, increased Fragmentation
493	 Index and WASO) for the SE group suggesting that sleep extension may have some
494	PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0273026 August 18, 2022 12 / 17
495	 PLOS ONE Sleep extension in rugby players
496	 detrimental effects on the subsequent night of sleep. Consequently, due to the potential diffi-
497	 culties to increase sleep acutely in the context of team sport, practitioners should consider
498	 keeping consistent sleep patterns and potentially add a post lunch nap during the day follow-
499	 ing a late exercise if a decrease in total sleep time is observed. Several studies have highlighted
500	 that when sleep restriction occurs, napping could be an efficient strategy to maintain total
501	 sleep time [1] but also performance [34, 35]. However, guidance regarding nap timing (e.g.
502	 between 13:00 to 16:00) and duration (e.g. <30min) need to be provided to the athletes [31].
503	 Moreover, the increase in fragmentation index, as well WASO was observed, suggesting that
504	 sleep was more disturbed in SE and may lead to restless sleep. Those results suggest that sleep
505	 quality should be improved concurrently to the sleep extension protocol. The importance of
506	 improving sleep quality is further reinforced by recent findings showing that collision activity
507	 could deteriorate sleep architecture [36].
508	 The effects of sleep extension and active recovery on recovery at POST 14
509	 The main results showed that SE affected cognitive function positively, although there was no
510	 improvement in recovery status of the lower body neuromuscular function at POST 14. Simi-
511	 larly, Fullagar et al. [9] found that an acute sleep hygiene strategy did not improve physical
512	 recovery after a football match. They hypothesised that neuromuscular function failed to
513	 improve because difference in terms of sleep quantity (i.e. total sleep time) was not sufficient
514	 (�1h). However, in the current study the effective difference in total sleep time between
515	 groups was much larger (� 02h30), but still did not result in any improvement in lower body
516	 neuromuscular function. This suggests that recovery of neuromuscular function following
517	 training and collision exposure is not sensitive to acute changes in total sleep time.
518	 The difference in cognitive function between groups in the current study is not surprising.
519	 It is well documented that sleep restriction has deleterious consequences for cognitive function
520	 [37]. The CON group’s total sleep time was low (� 04h30) which likely caused the large
521	 between group difference. Despite the absence of a substantial between group difference, HRR
522	 took longer to recover in the SE group. This suggests that the active recovery protocol may
523	 have had a positive effect on HRR by potentially improve parasympathetic activation [38].
524	 However, further research is required to show this conclusively.
525	 The mechanisms underpinning the differences between cognitive and physical recovery
526	 remain hypothetical. It has been shown that restricting sleep towards the end of the night
527	 reduces the proportion of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) while Non-REM (NREM) was con-
528	 served [39]. Those adjustments could explained the present results as NREM has been linked
529	 to cellular repair and energy storing while REM aims to improve cognitive processes [40]. In
530	 this study, the inclusion of an early morning session would have resulted in a reduction of
531	 REM proportion and therefore could explain the lack of difference on neuromuscular function
532	 as this suggests that the proportion of NREM was similar in both groups. However, results
533	 regarding professional football players showed that players went to bed later (i.e. �02:00 AM)
534	 than the present bedtime (i.e. midnight) observed in this study. While this is a realistic
535	 assumption, further research needs to explore the effect of different sleep restriction scenarios
536	 (morning vs. evening sleep restriction) and their respective effects on post-exercise recovery.
537	 Nevertheless, it is possible that a more targeted approach to enhance NREM could improve
538	 neuromuscular recovery as total sleep time did not seem to affect recovery positively or nega-
539	 tively. This necessity to improve NREM post-exercise is further strengthened by recent find-
540	 ings showing that the contact activity sustained during match may specifically decrease NREM
541	 [36]. Further research is required to understand how sleep extension may change sleep archi-
542	 tecture and consequently post-recovery kinetics.
543	PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0273026 August 18, 2022 13 / 17
544	 PLOS ONE Sleep extension in rugby players
545	 The effects of sleep extension and active recovery at POST 36
546	 While observing residual fatigue 30 hours following contact-based activity is normal [41], the
547	 absence of difference in recovery status was surprising. The absence of difference between groups
548	 could be due to the similar sleep instructions given to the players on night 2 facilitating CON
549	 group to pay back the acute sleep loss sustained. In turn, better subjective sleep quality and total
550	 sleep time were observed in CON group on night 2 compared to SE despite similar time in bed.
551	 This is characteristic of a sleep rebound observed after sleep restriction suggesting that the sleep
552	 pressure was more important in the CON group [42]. Indeed, due to the early scheduling of the
553	 recovery session, the CON group slept only 04h30. This behaviour might help CON group to
554	 counterbalance the negative effect of sleep restriction and explain the similar recovery status than
555	 SE at POST 36. Despite some positive effects at POST 14, active recovery did not show better
556	 effect at POST 36 which supports the notion that scheduling early active recovery remains contro-
557	 versial [14]. Practitioners should consequently avoid such practice scheduling and promote regu-
558	 lar sleep patterns instead as similar recovery status was observed. This is an important
559	 consideration because the cumulative load of these sessions over the course of a season contrib-
560	 utes to a substantial burden on staff and player’s time. It is possible that the positive effect
561	 observed at POST 14 could have been maintained or accentuated if the sleep extension protocol
562	 was prolonged over several nights as shown in previous studies [15, 43, 44]. Nevertheless, the
563	 implementation of all of these strategies is carefully related to the general team schedule. Staff
564	 members should be aware about the influence that they can have on sleep via the implementation
565	 of early recovery session. Future research should consider to extend sleep over the 2 days of the
566	 usual recovery cycle or the combination of active recovery and sleep extension in team sport.
567	 Limitations
568	 Despite the practical usefulness of actigraphy in the sport context, this method did not allow a
569	 measure of sleep architecture. Such a method would help to understand the difference between
570	 cognitive and physical recovery observed at POST 14 and potential link with sleep stages. Sec-
571	 ondly, baseline measurements showed that study participants were not achieving the recom-
572	 mend value of 7-9h of sleep per night [45]. Consequently, it is possible that participants
573	 contracted a sleep debt before the study and hide the potential effect of sleep extension. This
574	 further suggests that the recommended 10 hours of sleep might needs to be individualized
575	 based on the sleep profile (i.e. short vs. long sleeper). Finally, chronotype has not been investi-
576	 gated in this study. Preliminary analysis reported that all participants presented mid-range
577	 chronotype and therefore chronotype analysis could not be used in the present investigation.
578	 Future studies should consider including different chronotypes (morning vs. evening) and
579	 assess how it can impact sleep promoting strategies among athletes and post-exercise recovery.
580	 As it stands, it remains difficult to isolate the exact effect of sleep extension per se on recov-
581	 ery markers. The inclusion of a control group would have helped to ensure the exact effect of
582	 sleep extension compared with the active recovery strategy. While the inclusion of a control
583	 group remains always problematic in sport science research, the inclusion of active recovery
584	 within the sleep extension group would have helped to overcome this limitation. Further
585	 research will need to consider the effect of combined recovery (ice bath, active recovery) and
586	 sleep strategies on player status recovery.
587	 Practical applications
588	 • Sleep extension induces positive effects on cognitive function but not on neuromuscular
589	 function 14h following training.
590	PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0273026 August 18, 2022 14 / 17
591	 PLOS ONE Sleep extension in rugby players
592	 • Practitioners should carefully consider the scheduling of recovery session as it could be detri-
593	 mental to sleep. Therefore, if active recovery is performed, staff members should ensure it
594	 will not interfere with sleep.
595	 • At 36h following training, the recovery protocols were equally effective, and therefore the
596	 choice of recovery approach is a matter of athlete and practitioner preference.
597	 • Practitioners should be aware that they can have a direct impact on sleep by manipulating
598	 player’s training schedule.

 "sourceFile":"The effect of caffeine, nap opportunity and their combination on biomarkers of muscle damage and antioxidant defence during repeated sprint exercise.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",

 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The effect of caffeine, nap opportunity and their combination on biomarkers of muscle damage and antioxidant defence during repeated sprint exercise' (Biology of Sport 2022) matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain":"Recovery & Readiness",
 "domains":["Recovery & Readiness","Nutrition & Hydration","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Nutrition","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Combat Sports"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Double-blind, counterbalanced, randomised crossover study of 14 highly trained male judo athletes at international level (20 were screened). Four sessions, one week apart: placebo with no nap, a 20-minute nap with placebo, 5 mg/kg caffeine without a nap, and caffeine plus a 20-minute nap, followed by a running-based anaerobic sprint test. Compared with placebo, all treatments increased maximum and mean sprint power, and caffeine (with or without a nap) increased minimum power; post-exercise creatine kinase and urea rose with caffeine, and superoxide dismutase and glutathione peroxidase rose after napping.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only 14 male athletes, all caffeine-naive and non-habitual nappers, were tested in a laboratory repeated-sprint protocol that the authors say does not reflect field conditions. The study used one caffeine dose and a single 20-minute nap, and the authors caution that results may not carry over to regular caffeine users or female athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the higher sprint power and higher muscle-damage markers as a net benefit of caffeine, when the authors note muscle-damage markers also rose with caffeine.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Romdhani M, Souissi N, Dergaa I, Moussa-Chamari I, Chaabouni Y, Mahdouani K, et al. The effect of caffeine, nap opportunity and their combination on biomarkers of muscle damage and antioxidant defence during repeated sprint exercise. Biology of Sport. 2022;39(4):1033-1042.",
   "doi":"10.5114/biolsport.2023.112088",
   "abstract":"Fourteen highly trained male judo athletes completed four randomised, double-blind sessions: placebo with no nap, a 20-minute nap with placebo, 5 mg/kg caffeine, and caffeine plus a 20-minute nap. Repeated sprint power, plasma energy and muscle-damage markers, and antioxidant enzymes were measured around a running-based anaerobic sprint test.",
   "tldr":"A moderate caffeine dose (5 mg/kg) improved minimum sprint power and repeated sprint performance after a normal night's sleep, more than a 20-minute nap did. Caffeine also raised muscle-damage markers, while napping raised superoxide dismutase activity.",
   "methods":"Randomised, double-blind, counterbalanced crossover with 14 male international-level judo athletes, one week apart between sessions. Sessions were placebo, placebo with a 20-minute nap, caffeine (5 mg/kg), and caffeine with a nap, followed by the running-based anaerobic sprint test. Blood was sampled before and after exercise for lactate, glucose, creatine kinase, urea, AST, glutathione peroxidase and superoxide dismutase. Two-way repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni post hoc tests and Cohen's d were used.",
   "findings":"Compared with placebo, all treatments increased maximum and mean power on the sprint test (mean power rose by about 58 W with the nap, 90 W with caffeine and 128 W with caffeine plus nap, Table 2a). Minimum power was higher after caffeine and after caffeine plus nap than after the nap alone (mean difference 58.6 W and 102 W). Post-exercise creatine kinase and urea were higher with caffeine, and AST was higher after caffeine plus nap than after the nap alone. Superoxide dismutase rose versus placebo after the nap (p < 0.001) and after caffeine plus nap (p < 0.001), but not after caffeine alone. Glutathione peroxidase was not significant in the omnibus ANOVA or in any pairwise comparison against placebo in Table 2b. Plasma lactate rose only after the nap with placebo.",
   "limitations":"The sample was 14 male judo athletes, all caffeine-naive, which limits generalisation. The sprint test is a laboratory protocol and not sport-specific. The nap was subjectively timed. No female athletes were tested. The authors say a sleep-deprived study with the same caffeine dose found no benefit, so the result may depend on prior sleep. The Results text says glutathione peroxidase and superoxide dismutase rose only after napping, but Table 2b shows no significant glutathione peroxidase effect versus placebo; the table values were used here. The Discussion's explanations for the findings, such as aerobic glycolysis and sleep inertia, are not directly measured.",
   "practicalImplications":"In rested, caffeine-naive athletes, a 5 mg/kg caffeine dose improved repeated sprint performance more than a 20-minute nap. A nap alone improved maximum and mean sprint power but not minimum power. The caffeine-plus-nap combination gave the highest sprint performance in most participants. Caffeine also raised post-exercise muscle-damage markers, so staff should weigh that cost.",
   "athleteDev":"A 5 mg/kg caffeine dose before a repeated-sprint session can improve sprint power in rested, caffeine-naive athletes, and a short nap may add to this. Muscle-damage markers rose with caffeine, so the trade-off should be weighed. Results may not apply to habitual caffeine users.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot be used for return-to-play decisions. It tested healthy athletes in a laboratory sprint protocol and measured no injury or rehabilitation outcomes."
 }
}

ABSTRACT: To investigate the effect of 20 min nap opportunity (N20), 5 mg · kg-1 of caffeine (CAF) and their Tarak Driss
combination (CAF+N20) on the biochemical response (energetic biomarkers, biomarkers of muscle damage 0000-0001-6109-7393
and enzymatic antioxidants) to the running-based anaerobic sprint test. Fourteen highly trained male athletes
 Karim Chamari
completed in a double-blind, counterbalanced and randomized order four test sessions: no nap with placebo 0000-0001-9178-7678
(PLA), N20, CAF and CAF+N20. Compared to PLA, all treatments enhanced maximum and mean powers.
Minimum power was higher [(mean difference) 58.6 (95% confidence interval = 1.31–116) Watts] after CAF Omar Hammouda
 0000-0002-5002-687x
and [102 (29.9–175) Watts] after CAF+N20 compared to N20. Also, plasma glucose was higher after
CAF [0.81 (0.18–1.45) mmol · l-1] and CAF+N20 [1.03 (0.39–1.64) mmol · l-1] compared to N20. However, plasma
lactate was higher [1.64 (0.23–3.03) mmol · l-1] only after N20 compared to pre-exercise, suggesting a higher
anaerobic glycolysis during N20 compared to PLA, CAF and CAF+N20. Caffeine ingestion increased post-
exercise creatine kinase with [54.3 (16.7–91.1) IU · l-1] or without napping [58.9 (21.3–96.5) IU · l-1] compared
to PLA. However, superoxide dismutase was higher after napping with [339 (123–554) U · gHB-1] or without
caffeine [410 (195–625) U · gHB-1] compared to PLA. Probably because of the higher aerobic glycolysis contribution
in energy synthesis, caffeine ingestion resulted in better repeated sprint performance during CAF and CAF+N20
sessions compared to N20 and PLA. Caffeine ingestion resulted in higher muscle damage, and the short nap
enhanced antioxidant defence with or without caffeine ingestion.

 "evidenceSummary":"Prognostic cohort study of 75 elite young male football academy players from one Turkish Super League club, with radiological screening for cam and pincer morphology at pre-season or pre-transfer examinations and six seasons of injury data. Players with cam and/or pincer morphology (n = 23) had a higher hamstring injury rate than players without (14/23, 60.9% vs 18/52, 34.6%; p = 0.034). Recurrence (35.7% vs 27.8%, p = 0.631) and treatment duration (18.4 +/- 10.1 vs 12.1 +/- 6.2 days) were higher in the morphology group, but these differences were not statistically significant.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The morphology group was small (n = 23), and the two groups differed in age and body weight. Morphology was not separated into cam, pincer and mixed types, and the study has no kinematic or range-of-motion data, so it cannot show the mechanism.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the association as proof that cam and pincer morphology causes hamstring injury, when the study is a small single-club observational comparison with a significant unadjusted difference in injury rate.",

   "doi":"10.5152/j.aott.2023.22115",
   "abstract":"Seventy-five elite young male football academy players were screened radiologically for femoroacetabular impingement and followed for six seasons. Players with cam and/or pincer morphology (n = 23) were compared with those without (n = 52) for hamstring injury count, recurrence and treatment duration.",
   "tldr":"In one elite academy, young male football players with cam or pincer hip morphology had a higher rate of hamstring injury than players without it. Recurrence and time to return were higher too, but these differences were not statistically significant.",
   "methods":"Prospective data collection with retrospective analysis over six seasons in 75 elite young male academy players from one club. Hip morphology was assessed on pelvic radiographs at pre-season or pre-transfer examinations using alpha angle, lateral centre-edge angle and Tonnis angle criteria. Non-contact hamstring injuries, their treatment durations and recurrences were recorded. Chi-square and independent-samples t-tests were used, with P < 0.05 as significant.",
   "findings":"The hamstring injury rate was higher in players with cam and/or pincer morphology (14 of 23, 60.9%) than without (18 of 52, 34.6%; p = 0.034). Recurrence was 35.7% (5 of 14) vs 27.8% (5 of 18), p = 0.631. Treatment duration was 18.4 +/- 10.1 days vs 12.1 +/- 6.2 days, which was not significant. Morphology players were older (20.35 vs 18.92 years) and heavier (71.5 vs 67.7 kg), and these differences were significant.",
   "limitations":"The morphology group was small (n = 23) and the two groups differed in age and body weight, which were not adjusted for. Cam, pincer and mixed morphologies were grouped together, and the sample was one male academy in one country. Range of motion and muscle-length data were not collected. The Results text gives 60.09% for injury in the morphology group, but 14 of 23 is 60.9%, which matches Table 2. Figure 1 treatment durations are not significant.",
   "practicalImplications":"Screening for cam and pincer morphology could help identify young football players who may have a higher hamstring injury rate, so staff may want to monitor them more closely. The study does not show that morphology causes injury or that it changes recovery time. Hip morphology alone should not be used to decide training load or playing availability.",
   "athleteDev":"Young players with cam or pincer morphology may warrant closer hamstring monitoring and prevention work. This is an association from one academy, so it should guide monitoring rather than set training prescriptions.",
   "rtp":"The study reports time to return after hamstring injury, but the difference was not significant and the sample was small. It cannot set return-to-play criteria or show that morphology should change clearance timing."

 "evidenceSummary":"Systematic review and three meta-analyses (exercise performance, end core temperature, submaximal core temperature) of 25 peer-reviewed controlled studies of dietary supplements during endurance exercise in hot conditions (at least 30 C), with searches in PubMed and SPORTDiscus in May 2020. Participants were healthy adults (18 years or older), with training and acclimation status varying across studies. Supplementation had a trivial, statistically significant positive effect on performance (Hedges g = 0.18, 95% CI 0.007 to 0.352, p = 0.042), and non-significant small effects on core temperature. Caffeine raised end core temperature (g = 0.82, n = 8), and taurine lowered it (g = -0.96, n = 1).",
 "screeningLimitations":"Most included studies were controlled laboratory trials of short, mostly acute protocols, and several supplement subgroups had only one or a few studies. The sample is healthy adults rather than athletes specifically, so the findings are general to hot-environment exercise.",

   "year":2021,
   "citation":"Peel JS, McNarry MA, Heffernan SM, Nevola VR, Kilduff LP, Waldron M. The Effect of Dietary Supplements on Endurance Exercise Performance and Core Temperature in Hot Environments: A Meta-analysis and Meta-regression. Sports Medicine. 2021.",
   "doi":"10.1007/s40279-021-01500-2",
   "abstract":"Systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 controlled studies of dietary supplements on endurance performance and core temperature in the heat, with meta-regression on moderating variables. Supplements were selected for strong evidence in thermoneutral conditions or a plausible thermal mechanism.",
   "tldr":"Across 25 hot-environment studies, dietary supplements gave only a trivial performance benefit. Caffeine raised core temperature, and the amino acid results were non-significant, so current heat guidance may need revision.",
   "methods":"PRISMA-guided search of PubMed and SPORTDiscus (May 2020), with two reviewers screening independently. Eligible studies were controlled crossover, randomised or independent-group designs with healthy adults aged 18 or older, exhaustive endurance exercise of at least 75 s, and ambient temperature of at least 30 C. Three random-effects meta-analyses (performance, end core temperature, submaximal core temperature) and meta-regressions of moderators were run in RStudio, with effects reported as Hedges g. The 25 studies included 272 participants (88% male, 56% highly trained), 24 with crossover designs.",
   "findings":"Overall, supplementation had a trivial, significant positive effect on performance (g = 0.18, 95% CI 0.007 to 0.352, p = 0.042). Its effects on submaximal core temperature (g = 0.18) and end core temperature (g = 0.20) were small and non-significant. Caffeine had a large positive effect on end core temperature (g = 0.82, 95% CI 0.433 to 1.202, n = 8), and taurine had a medium negative effect (g = -0.96, n = 1). Amino acids had small to medium but non-significant performance effects (BCAAs g = 0.32, tyrosine g = 0.21, taurine g = 0.55). Most moderators, including heat acclimation, training status and hydration, did not explain variation.",
   "limitations":"Most included studies were controlled laboratory trials, mostly acute supplementation, with only nine trials longer than one hour. Several supplement subgroups had only one or a few studies, and the taurine finding rests on one study. Egger's test indicated publication bias in the end core temperature analysis (P = 0.015), and trim-and-fill made no meaningful adjustment, so the end core temperature estimates may be inflated; several outliers were also detected in that analysis. The authors note that most studies recruited non-acclimated, hydrated participants, which limits the moderator analysis. Participants were healthy adults rather than athletes specifically.",
   "practicalImplications":"Caffeine and nitrate did not show a clear performance benefit in hot conditions, and caffeine raised core temperature, so staff should monitor heat strain when it is used. Amino acid and taurine results are too limited to recommend. The authors suggest current heat-performance guidance may need revision, but the evidence base is small.",
   "athleteDev":"In hot conditions, caffeine may raise core temperature without a clear performance gain, so its use should be weighed against heat-strain risk. Evidence for amino acids and taurine is too thin to base a recommendation on.",
   "rtp":"This review cannot be used for return-to-play decisions. It concerns healthy adults' endurance performance in heat and includes no injured or rehabilitating participants."

6	and Meta‑regression

8	Mark Waldron1,3,4
9	Accepted: 2 June 2021
10	© The Author(s) 2021
11	Abstract
12	Background The ergogenic effects of dietary supplements on endurance exercise performance are well-established; however,
13	their efficacy in hot environmental conditions has not been systematically evaluated.
14	Objectives (1) To meta-analyse studies investigating the effects of selected dietary supplements on endurance performance
15	and core temperature responses in the heat. Supplements were included if they were deemed to: (a) have a strong evidence
16	base for ‘directly’ improving thermoneutral endurance performance, based on current position statements, or (b) have a
17	proposed mechanism of action that related to modifiable factors associated with thermal balance. (2) To conduct meta-
18	regressions to evaluate the moderating effect of selected variables on endurance performance and core temperature responses
19	in the heat following dietary supplementation.
20	Methods A search was performed using various databases in May 2020. After screening, 25 peer-reviewed articles were
21	identified for inclusion, across three separate meta-analyses: (1) exercise performance; (2) end core temperature; (3) sub-
22	maximal core temperature. The moderating effect of several variables were assessed via sub-analysis and meta-regression.
23	Results Overall, dietary supplementation had a trivial significant positive effect on exercise performance (Hedges’ g = 0.18,
24	95% CI 0.007–0.352, P = 0.042), a trivial non-significant positive effect on submaximal core temperature (Hedges’ g = 0.18,
25	95% CI − 0.021 to 0.379, P = 0.080) and a small non-significant positive effect on end core temperature (Hedges’ g = 0.20,
26	95% CI − 0.041 to 0.439, P = 0.104) in the heat. There was a non-significant effect of individual supplements on exercise
27	performance (P = 0.973) and submaximal core temperature (P = 0.599). However, end core temperature was significantly
28	affected by supplement type (P = 0.003), which was attributable to caffeine’s large significant positive effect (n = 8; Hedges’
29	g = 0.82, 95% CI 0.433–1.202, P < 0.001) and taurine’s medium significant negative effect (n = 1; Hedges’ g = − 0.96, 95%
30	CI − 1.855 to − 0.069, P = 0.035).
31	Conclusion Supplements such as caffeine and nitrates do not enhance endurance performance in the heat, with caffeine also
32	increasing core temperature responses. Some amino acids might offer the greatest performance benefits in the heat. Exercis-
33	ing in the heat negatively affected the efficacy of many dietary supplements, indicating that further research is needed and
34	current guidelines for performance in hot environments likely require revision.

 SYSTEMATIC REVIEW
The Effect of Dietary Supplements on Endurance Exercise Performance
and Core Temperature in Hot Environments: A Meta‑analysis
and Meta‑regression
Jennifer S. Peel1 · Melitta A. McNarry1 · Shane M. Heffernan1 · Venturino R. Nevola1,2 · Liam P. Kilduff1,3 ·
Mark Waldron1,3,4
Accepted: 2 June 2021
© The Author(s) 2021
Abstract
Background The ergogenic effects of dietary supplements on endurance exercise performance are well-established; however,
their efficacy in hot environmental conditions has not been systematically evaluated.
Objectives (1) To meta-analyse studies investigating the effects of selected dietary supplements on endurance performance
and core temperature responses in the heat. Supplements were included if they were deemed to: (a) have a strong evidence
base for ‘directly’ improving thermoneutral endurance performance, based on current position statements, or (b) have a
proposed mechanism of action that related to modifiable factors associated with thermal balance. (2) To conduct meta-
regressions to evaluate the moderating effect of selected variables on endurance performance and core temperature responses
in the heat following dietary supplementation.
Methods A search was performed using various databases in May 2020. After screening, 25 peer-reviewed articles were
identified for inclusion, across three separate meta-analyses: (1) exercise performance; (2) end core temperature; (3) sub-
maximal core temperature. The moderating effect of several variables were assessed via sub-analysis and meta-regression.
Results Overall, dietary supplementation had a trivial significant positive effect on exercise performance (Hedges’ g = 0.18,
95% CI 0.007–0.352, P = 0.042), a trivial non-significant positive effect on submaximal core temperature (Hedges’ g = 0.18,
95% CI − 0.021 to 0.379, P = 0.080) and a small non-significant positive effect on end core temperature (Hedges’ g = 0.20,
95% CI − 0.041 to 0.439, P = 0.104) in the heat. There was a non-significant effect of individual supplements on exercise
performance (P = 0.973) and submaximal core temperature (P = 0.599). However, end core temperature was significantly
affected by supplement type (P = 0.003), which was attributable to caffeine’s large significant positive effect (n = 8; Hedges’
g = 0.82, 95% CI 0.433–1.202, P < 0.001) and taurine’s medium significant negative effect (n = 1; Hedges’ g = − 0.96, 95%
CI − 1.855 to − 0.069, P = 0.035).
Conclusion Supplements such as caffeine and nitrates do not enhance endurance performance in the heat, with caffeine also
increasing core temperature responses. Some amino acids might offer the greatest performance benefits in the heat. Exercis-
ing in the heat negatively affected the efficacy of many dietary supplements, indicating that further research is needed and
current guidelines for performance in hot environments likely require revision.

{
 "id":"Q62",
 "sourceFile":"The effect of exercise-induced fatigue and heat exposure on soccer-specific decision-making during high intensity intermittent exercise.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The effect of exercise-induced fatigue and heat exposure on soccer-specific decision-making during high-intensity intermittent exercise' (PLOS ONE 2022) matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains":["Brain Health & Psychology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Soccer"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Laboratory study of nine well-trained male soccer players who completed a 92-minute cycling intermittent sprint protocol at 32 C (hot) and 18 C (temperate), responding to soccer-specific decision-making trials during the protocol. Decision-making scores were lower in the heat (86.87 +/- 7.95% vs 92.49 +/- 3.13%, p = 0.030), with no condition by time interaction. Power output fell in the second half only in the heat, and plasma normetanephrine and metanephrine rose more in the heat. Ten players were planned, but testing stopped early because of the pandemic, so trial order was not fully counterbalanced.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only nine players were analysed, the trial order was only partly counterbalanced, and the protocol used cycling rather than running. The decision-making task was a single visual task, and no interaction effect was found, so the timing of the decline is uncertain.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the lower decision-making scores as a clear hot-weather effect on match decision-making, when the interaction was not significant and the sample was nine players in a cycling-based protocol.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Donnan KJ, Williams EL, Stanger N. The effect of exercise-induced fatigue and heat exposure on soccer-specific decision-making during high-intensity intermittent exercise. PLoS ONE. 2022;17(12):e0279109.",
   "doi":"10.1371/journal.pone.0279109",
   "abstract":"Nine well-trained male soccer players completed a 92-minute cycling intermittent sprint protocol at 32 C (hot) and 18 C (temperate), responding to soccer-specific decision-making trials throughout. Physical output, decision-making, appraisal, affect and plasma metanephrines were measured.",
   "tldr":"In nine trained soccer players, heat lowered soccer-specific decision-making during a prolonged intermittent sprint protocol. Power output also fell in the second half only in the heat, with a more threatening appraisal and higher stress hormone levels.",
   "methods":"Laboratory study with nine well-trained male soccer players, planned as a counterbalanced design for 10 players but stopped early because of the pandemic (five players began in 32 C, four in 18 C). Participants completed a 92-minute cycling intermittent sprint protocol, with the high-intensity workload set from their own VO2max test, at 32 C and 50% relative humidity or 18 C and 50% relative humidity. Soccer-specific decision-making was scored against expert panel responses and verbal think-aloud reports were coded. Analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and content analysis.",
   "findings":"Decision-making scores were lower in 32 C than 18 C (86.87 +/- 7.95% vs 92.49 +/- 3.13%, main effect p = 0.030), but there was no condition by time interaction. Power output fell in the second half of the protocol only in the heat (about 7%). Plasma normetanephrine was higher at half-time (p = 0.012) and post-exercise (p < 0.001), and metanephrine was higher post-exercise (p = 0.009), with larger rises in the heat. Players verbalised less future planning in the heat, and threat appraisal and unpleasant affect were higher in the heat (p = 0.007 and p = 0.008).",
   "limitations":"Only nine players were analysed, and the planned 10 were not reached. Trial order was only partly counterbalanced. A cycling protocol was used, which the authors say may produce less physiological strain than running. The decision-making task was visual only and did not reproduce dual-task demands of match play. Laboratory motivation may differ from matches. The think-aloud findings need caution given the number of analyses run. Core temperature averaged about 38.4 C in the heat, and the authors say this is lower than typical team-sport values.",
   "practicalImplications":"In hot conditions, soccer players may make poorer decisions and lose work output, even when core temperature stays below common cut-offs. Staff planning training or matches in heat should consider decision-making as well as physical output. Players also reported more threat and unpleasant feelings in the heat, so coaches may want to address that in preparation.",
   "athleteDev":"Heat can lower decision-making and second-half work output during intermittent exercise, even when core temperature stays around 38.4 C. Coaches should plan heat-exposure training and tactical work with this in mind.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot be used for return-to-play decisions. It tested healthy trained players in a laboratory cycling protocol and includes no injury or rehabilitation outcomes."
 }
}

58	ac.uk. ception and correct interpretation of information from the environment, and the selection of

60	funding for this work. racy [6]. Although effective decision-making and sporting intelligence will aid a soccer player
61	Competing interests: The authors have declared in making correct decisions from a variety of stimuli (e.g., identification of space, predicting
62	that no competing interests exist. opposition movement and receiving/giving instructions), the execution of such cognitive skills
63	 is also dependent upon other factors whilst competing, including the onset of fatigue [7].
64	 During the physically demanding nature of competitive soccer, physical fatigue occurs due
65	 to a depletion in energy stores (i.e., glycogen), increased thermal strain, dehydration, and the
66	 alteration of central mechanisms (e.g., neurochemical change) [8]. Soccer players cover less
67	 distance [9] and skilled performance has been shown to deteriorate in the second half, com-
68	 pared to the first half of match-play [10]. However, fatigue has also been associated with altered
69	 perceptual states and impaired central nervous system functioning [11] that can impact deci-
70	 sion-making ability.
71	 Research in team sport has shown that high-intensity or prolonged exercise can improve
72	 decision-making speed [12,13], but may impair decision-making accuracy or quality [e.g.,
73	 13,14]. These effects have been linked to variations in arousal [15] induced by physiological
74	 changes (e.g., plasma catecholamines, cortical activation) at central and peripheral levels [16].
75	 That said, some reviews have highlighted ambiguous findings whereby no effects or positive
76	 effects of high-intensity or prolonged exercise on cognitive function have been found [e.g., 17–
77	 19]. Such variations in findings may be explained by differences in methodologies such as the
78	 timing of cognitive function. Based on premises of the ‘transient hypofrontality hypothesis’,
79	 during demanding physical work, neural resources are re-directed away from pre-frontal areas
80	 of the brain responsible for higher-order (or more complex) cognitive functioning, to areas of
81	 the brain responsible for maintaining motor control to prioritise maintenance of physical
82	 work. [20]. However, when exercise has abated neural resources are suggested to be re-directed
83	 back toward pre-frontal areas [20]. Thus, differences in methodologies such as the timing and
84	 complexity of cognitive task implemented (i.e., pre- to post- exercise, or during) can influence
85	 the effects that exercise can have cognitive function, which could explain some of the varied
86	 observations in previous research. Additionally, the decision-making tasks employed in most
87	 studies to date are not situation-specific, thus they can be more predictable than decisions
88	 faced within match-play and have limited ecological validity. Therefore, research investigating
89	 the effects of incremental fatigue on sport-specific decision-making during exercise warrants
90	 further attention.
91	 As well as the typical incremental fatigue experienced during competitive soccer matches in
92	 thermoneutral environments, athletes can be required to perform in hot environments, such
93	 as during pre-season and international tournaments [e.g., 2022 Qatar FIFA World Cup, 21].
94	 Performing in high environmental temperatures can exacerbate the physiological and percep-
95	 tual strain experienced during match-play such as increased core temperature (TC), cardiovas-
96	 cular strain (e.g., increased heart rate), dehydration, and neurochemical alterations [22,23],
97	 resulting in physical [24] and cognitive [e.g., 25,26] performance decrements.
98	 Previous research has also revealed that physiological load or the incremental fatigue expe-
99	 rienced during exercise could also disrupt one’s attention during sporting performance. For
100	 instance, Casanova et al. [27] found that increased physiological loads caused soccer players’
101	 attention to be directed to task-irrelevant cues more often, resulting in reduced anticipation
102	 accuracy. ‘Think-aloud’ retrospective reports exploring how expert players used situational
103	 information when making anticipation judgments, showed that deep planning statements
104	 decreased from early in the first half, to the end of the first half and second half of soccer-spe-
105	 cific activity. This reflected a deterioration in higher level thought processing with fatigue,
106	PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0279109 December 15, 2022 2 / 24
107	 PLOS ONE Exercise-induced fatigue and heat on soccer-specific decision-making during exercise
108	 which may be further impaired under additional physiological strain induced by heat expo-
109	 sure. However, research employing such ‘think aloud’ methods to understand athletes’ reason-
110	 ing for decisions as a result of incremental fatigue is limited. Indeed, researchers have yet to
111	 examine the effect that heat exposure can have on such thought processes in athletes during
112	 exercise that is reflective of the physiological load experienced during match-play.
113	 It is possible that heat stress and incremental fatigue can also impact an athlete’s appraisal
114	 of the activity demands, and previous research has revealed that it can result in more unpleas-
115	 ant affective states [e.g., 14], which could also be linked with physical and cognitive perfor-
116	 mance. The Theory of Challenge and Threat States in Athletes [TCTSA; 28] offers insights into
117	 how athletic performance may be impacted by competitive stress and the appraisal of an activ-
118	 ity. It is suggested that a challenge state is usually (but not always) associated with positively
119	 valenced emotions as well as linked with effective decision-making, higher task engagement,
120	 and positive performance. In contrast, a threat state is suggested to be associated with (typi-
121	 cally) negatively valenced emotions as well as emotions that are perceived as unhelpful for per-
122	 formance, impaired cognitive functioning, reduced task engagement and performance
123	 decrements [28].
124	 The TCTSA also identifies physiological responses associated with the appraisal of an activ-
125	 ity. Increased sympathetic-adrenal medulla (SAM) activity is proposed to represent a challenge
126	 state, whereas a threat state is posited to be characterised by increased SAM and pituitary-adre-
127	 nal cortical (PAC) activity, both of which are affected by heat exposure. Specifically, acute heat
128	 stress has been shown to increase both SAM activity (e.g., increased release of epinephrine and
129	 norepinephrine) and PAC activity (e.g., increased adrenocorticotropic hormone and cortisol
130	 release) [29]. Therefore, where SAM and PAC activity increase in response to acute heat stress
131	 [29], performing strenuous activity in hot environments may also contribute to athletes’
132	 appraising activity as more threatening compared to temperate conditions [28]. To the
133	 authors’ knowledge, only one study has tested and found that heat exposure during intermit-
134	 tent exercise can make athletes feel more unpleasant compared to temperate conditions [14],
135	 and researchers have yet to directly investigate whether heat exposure could also influence ath-
136	 letes’ appraisal during prolonged high-intensity intermittent exercise. Such examination
137	 would offer novel insights about how heat exposure can influence appraisal and affective states
138	 during exercise in the heat, which could help inform approaches to assist athletes coping when
139	 performing in hot conditions.
140	 Purpose of the research
141	 To date, no research has investigated the effects of prolonged intermittent exercise and heat
142	 exposure on soccer players’ decision-making. Moreover, through the implementation of
143	 ‘think-aloud’ protocols [e.g., 27], it is known that fatigue can impair higher level thought pro-
144	 cessing in soccer players. However, to date, no study has yet to explore how the additional
145	 stress imposed by heat exposure may impact such processes. Additionally, research has yet to
146	 investigate how heat exposure during prolonged intermittent exercise reflective of physical
147	 demands of match-play can affect a combination of biological (i.e., epinephrine and norepi-
148	 nephrine) and psychological (i.e., changes to affect, appraisal) responses that could have a role
149	 to play on performance (e.g., 28) in soccer players.
150	 Therefore, the aim of this research was to examine how heat exposure (32˚C) during pro-
151	 longed intermittent sprint exercise affected physical work output, soccer-specific decision-
152	 making, demand and resource appraisals (i.e., challenge and threat), affective valence (i.e., pos-
153	 itive or negative feelings), and plasma metanephrines (i.e., plasma metanephrine and normeta-
154	 nephrine, as serum metabolite indicators of epinephrine and norepinephrine, respectively), in
155	PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0279109 December 15, 2022 3 / 24
156	 PLOS ONE Exercise-induced fatigue and heat on soccer-specific decision-making during exercise
157	 comparison to a temperate condition (18˚C). As it was expected that soccer players would be
158	 under greater physiological and psychological strain in the heat, the following hypotheses were
159	 tested. First, it was hypothesised that power output (measure of physical output) and the qual-
160	 ity of decision-making would deteriorate during the later stages of the protocol as a result of
161	 exercise-induced fatigue, and that this deterioration would be more pronounced in 32˚C com-
162	 pared to 18˚C (H1). Second, it was anticipated that during exercise in 32˚C, players’ ability to
163	 engage in higher level thought processes would be reduced when retrospectively evaluating
164	 their decision, compared to during exercise at 18˚C (H2). Third, it was expected that threat
165	 appraisal about the activity demands, and unpleasant affect, would be higher in 32˚C com-
166	 pared to 18˚C (H3). Finally, it was believed that metanephrine and normetanephrine levels
167	 would increase in response to exercise, but more significantly in the hot, compared to the tem-
168	 perate conditions, reflecting a heightened physiological stress response (H4).
169	 Materials and methods
170	 Participants
171	 Nine well-trained male soccer players at a university in the United Kingdom (M ± SD
172	 age = 19.89 ± 0.78 years; body fat = 11.94 ± 0.04%) with an average of 13.11 (± 1.45) years of
173	 experience competing in soccer were recruited. The highest competition standard ranged
174	 across national (n = 2), regional (n = 3) and club (n = 4) levels. An estimated sample size of
175	 nine participants was determined by a power calculation using G� Power 3.1.9.4 [30], applying
176	 an estimated large effect (i.e., Cohen’s d = 1.1; f = 0.55) with power (1- β = .80) and significance
177	 (alpha = .05). The effect size coefficient applied was based on the results from a study which
178	 examined the effects of exercise on cognition between hot (36˚C) and temperate (20˚C) condi-
179	 tions, which found such (large) effects and significant differences for changes in cognitive per-
180	 formance (random movement generation) from pre-exercise to immediately post-exercise
181	 between temperature conditions in a sample of 8 participants [31].
182	 Participants were asked to refrain from ergogenic aids for the duration of the study and
183	 should not have performed strenuous exercise in >30˚C for at least 3 months prior [32]. Par-
184	 ticipants were non-smokers, with no history of cardiovascular or respiratory problems. They
185	 were asked to standardize their food intake on the morning of each trial, abstain from alcohol
186	 and caffeine for �24 hours, refrain from strenuous exercise for �48 hours, and maintain their
187	 regular sleep pattern for �72 hours [32]. A food (including photographs) and sleep diary was
188	 completed by each participant in the 48-hours leading to each trial to ensure standardisation
189	 was met. Participants arrived �2 hours post-prandial and consumed between 2–3 litres of
190	 water in the 24 hours leading to testing. Following approval from Leeds Beckett University
191	 research ethics committee, all eligible participants provided written consent before commenc-
192	 ing testing.
193	 Experimental design and procedure
194	 In total, participants visited the laboratory on five occasions over a 28-day period. The first
195	 visit was for familiarisation and the remaining four trials were separated into two parts for dif-
196	 ferent purposes. Specifically, experimental trials 1 and 2 (Part A) were used to explore the psy-
197	 chological, biological, and decision-making implications of exercising in hot compared to
198	 temperate conditions, whereas trials 3 and 4 (Part B) were used to explore the effectiveness of
199	 Tyrosine supplementation for performing in hot conditions. Due to the extensiveness of the
200	 research undertaken, this article focuses only on Part A. Thus, a 2 × condition within-subjects
201	 design was employed whereby participants completed trials in a temperate (18˚C; 50% relative
202	 humidity [rh]) and hot (32˚C; 50% rh) condition. With the aim of using a fully
203	PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0279109 December 15, 2022 4 / 24
204	 PLOS ONE Exercise-induced fatigue and heat on soccer-specific decision-making during exercise
205	 counterbalanced design, we intended to include 10 participants. However, due to the global
206	 pandemic, testing was terminated early. Therefore, 5 participants completed their first trial in
207	 32˚C, whilst 4 completed their first trial in 18˚C. Results for 8 participants when conditions
208	 were fully counterbalanced can be found in the Support Information. Trial days were kept �2
209	 to �7 days apart and testing times remained consistent to control for circadian variation and
210	 subsequent effects on core temperature and power output [33,34].
211	 During the first visit, participants completed an incremental exercise test on a cycle ergom-
212	 eter to determine power output at VO2max [35]. Once recovered, participants were instructed
213	 to watch 10 soccer-specific clips and respond verbally as to what they would do next if they
214	 were in possession of the ball and provide reasoning for their decision. This was to familiarise
215	 participants with a newly validated decision-making protocol (detailed below). Participants
216	 were then familiarised with the cannulation process before completing a standardised warm-
217	 up, followed by 10 × 5-s sprints of the Cycling Intermittent Sprint Protocol (CISP) (20 min) to
218	 familiarise with the protocol. Simultaneous decision-making tasks (and verbal reports) were
219	 completed following every other sprint during this process. Participants then spent a short
220	 period of time (~5-min) sat in the chamber at *30˚C to minimise any potential negative emo-
221	 tional reactions to the heat during trials.
222	 The next laboratory visits comprised of the experimental conditions. For each visit, partici-
223	 pants were provided with food vouchers, allowing them to replicate what they consumed for
224	 breakfast and lunch on the first trial day on all subsequent visits. Ad libitum water intake was
225	 permitted between the 22nd-28th-min, and between the 62nd-68th-min of the CISP, to replicate
226	 water breaks during major soccer competitions held in >30˚C [36], and total consumption
227	 (ml) was recorded. To facilitate a competitive element and incentivise effort during the trials, a
228	 financial incentive was included [e.g., 37]. Participants were informed that the player who had
229	 the highest combined average decision-making score as well as physical performance across
230	 trials would be awarded a £100 cash prize.
231	 Maximal oxygen uptake (VO2max). To determine power at VO2max, during the familiari-
232	 sation visit participants were instructed to cycle at a pedal rate between 70–90 rpm. One min-
233	 ute at 75W was performed, after which work rate increased at a rate of 25W.min-1 until
234	 participants cadence declined by >10 rpm or through volitional exhaustion. Breath-by-breath
235	 pulmonary gas exchange was collected throughout (Cortex, Metalyzer 3B) and data was aver-
236	 aged across 10-s periods. The VO2max was identified as the highest 30-s mean value attained
237	 before the point of volitional exhaustion [e.g., 38]. The power output at the point of volitional
238	 exhaustion was then used to inform the protocol in the main trials (see details below). Heart
239	 rate (HR) was measured throughout via a Polar HR monitor (FT1, Polar, Finland) and subse-
240	 quently averaged for each incremental stage.
241	 Cycling intermittent sprint protocol (CISP). An extended version of the CISP [39] (see
242	 Fig 1) was used whereby it was increased to 46-min (23 sprints) from the original 40-min (20
243	 sprints), per half, to better reflect the duration of soccer matches. Each trial consisted of a
244	 warm-up of 5-min cycling at 95W at 80 rpm, followed by two 30-s periods of passive rest inter-
245	 spersed with 30-s cycling at 120W [40]. The extended CISP consisted of 23 blocks of 2-min
246	 periods in each half consisting of a 5-s maximal sprint against a resistance of 8% body mass
247	 (BM), 105-s of active recovery at 35% VO2peak calculated from the familiarisation visit, fol-
248	 lowed by 10-s passive rest [39]. Each half of the CISP was interspersed with a 15-min “half-
249	 time” period involving passive recovery in a temperate environment (~18˚C). Therefore, each
250	 trial comprised of a total of 46 blocks of 2-min to simulate the demands of a typical competi-
251	 tive soccer match [41].
252	PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0279109 December 15, 2022 5 / 24
253	 PLOS ONE Exercise-induced fatigue and heat on soccer-specific decision-making during exercise
254	 Fig 1. A schematic showing a modified version of one half of the extended Cycling Intermittent Sprint Protocol [39,40].
255	 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0279109.g001
256	 Main outcome measures
257	 Peak power output (PPO). PPO (W) was determined as the highest power output
258	 recorded during each sprint of the CISP [39]. Lode Ergometry Manager (Version 10, Lode,
259	 Groningen, The Netherlands) automatically recorded these outputs following every sprint and
260	 this data was then transferred to Excel (Version 2008, Microsoft). These outputs were averaged
261	 per half of the CISP to analyse differences between the first and second half of match-play.
262	 Decision-making. Within the trials, decision-making was assessed by asking participants
263	 to watch video clips and decide what their next choice would be for the player in possession of
264	 the ball. Clips were cut from previous 2014 and 2018 World Cup footage using Adobe Premier
265	 Pro (Adobe Inc, California, United States). Similar to previous research [27], clips lasted for
266	 *5 seconds and froze just before the player in possession of the ball executed their decision
267	 (e.g., shoot). At this point, participants were asked what they would do next. Prior to imple-
268	 mentation in the present study, the decision-making protocol was validated in a preliminary
269	 study involving an ethically approved, three-stage process.
270	 Development of decision-making protocol. The first stage of the validation process aimed to
271	 test the face and content validity of the clips, which involved four well-trained adult soccer
272	 players (2 men; 2 women) reviewing a total of 205 clips to assess (a) the clarity of the clips
273	 (from 1 = not at all clear, to, 9 = extremely clear), (b) ensure that a minimum of 3 realistic
274	 response options were available (e.g., pass, cross, dribble, clear, turn, shoot), and (c) rank the
275	 difficulty of making a decision from the clip (from 1 = very easy, to, 9 = very difficult). Frequent
276	 breaks were included to reduce fatigue. This process resulted in 5 clips being removed based
277	 on an insufficient number of options.
278	 The second stage aimed to further support the face validity of the remaining clips and
279	 develop a scoring system based on an expert panel of four UEFA qualified coaches (including
280	 an ex-international player) who independently ranked what would be the best, second best
281	 and third best option in each clip. The expert panel also rated the perceived difficulty of the
282	 decision as per stage one, and breaks were again included to reduce fatigue. Based on this pro-
283	 cess, four options remained for the decision-making; namely “maintaining possession” (e.g.,
284	 drive, turn), “pass” (including crossing), “clear”, and “shoot”. Following this process, the bank
285	 of clips was cut to 84, with only those with the highest agreement scores (e.g., �90% score,
286	 where a minimum of three experts had rated the same best available option, with one expert
287	 rating this as the second best) remaining, alongside accounting for clip difficulty. As partici-
288	 pants completed four CISP trials in this research (two trials to address the aims in the present
289	PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0279109 December 15, 2022 6 / 24
290	 PLOS ONE Exercise-induced fatigue and heat on soccer-specific decision-making during exercise
291	 study), the clips were split into 4 × sets of 21 clips of similar difficulty, distributing easy, mod-
292	 erate, and difficult clips evenly across sets of footage, as based on expert judgements. For each
293	 overall set, three clips were intended to be used for pre-exercise, then nine clips for each half of
294	 the CISP (i.e., 3 + 9 + 9 = 21 clips). Reliability analyses were conducted to confirm that the
295	 experts’ judgement scores were similar across the 4 sets of clips (Fleiss kappa >.80), and across
296	 the block of 3 clips (intended for pre-exercise) and 2 blocks of 9 clips (intended for each half of
297	 the CISP) within each of the four sets (Fleiss kappa > .80).
298	 The third stage involved a sample of 14 well-trained outfield female soccer players complet-
299	 ing the decision protocol at rest, to test that the scoring for the decision-making clips did not
300	 differ between the 4 sets of 21 clips nor between the blocks of 3 clips (for pre-exercise) and 9
301	 clips (for each half of the CISP). Indeed, analyses revealed no set × block interactions (F6,78 =
302	 .676, p = .669, ηp2 = .049), nor differences between sets of clips (F3,39 = 1.114, p = .355, ηp2 =
303	 .079), or across blocks (F1.295.16.835 = 2.374, p = .138, ηp2 = .154). Post-hoc analysis was run
304	 using LSD as the least conservative approach for observing differences and no post-hoc differ-
305	 ences were found between any block within sets (ps = .189 to .932) or between sets (ps = .169
306	 to .672). Overall, supporting that the sets of clips were not different in scoring at rest, and
307	 thereby suitable to be randomly allocated for the main experimental trials to determine any
308	 differences in decision-making between conditions.
309	 Decision-making in the present study. Pre-exercise decision-making was measured by par-
310	 ticipants responding to 3 decision-making clips (each lasting 5-seconds). A further 9 clips in
311	 each half of the CISP were used to assess decision-making during exercise. These were regu-
312	 larly presented in 3 sets of 3 clips in each half and implemented at the same respective time
313	 points for each half (see Fig 1).
314	 After each decision-making clip, the final frame froze for 3-seconds where participants
315	 were asked to provide their verbal response as to what they would do next if they were the
316	 player in possession of the ball. Participants had four initial choices when making their deci-
317	 sion; “pass”, “shoot”, “clear”, and “maintain possession” and were asked to verbally respond as
318	 quickly and accurately as possible. If pass was selected, participants were then asked which
319	 player they intended to pass to by identifying the colour of the circle around the chosen player.
320	 Based on the rankings from experts in the preliminary study, participants were awarded 3
321	 points for the best option, 2 points for the second-best option, and 1 point for any other
322	 response given from any of the expert panel during the validation process. Therefore, 9 points
323	 were available pre-CISP (from the 3 clips), and a maximum of 27 points were available for
324	 each half of the CISP (from the 9 clips). For analysis, an average percentage was taken to pro-
325	 vide a decision-making score, which was calculated for pre-CISP, the first half, and second half,
326	 of the CISP.
327	 After responding initially, participants had 30-s where they were asked to evaluate their
328	 response during active recovery. Specifically, participants were asked to provide a reason for
329	 their choice, drawing on anything which helped influence their decision such as space, player
330	 movement and what could happen next. This method was informed by similar “think-aloud”
331	 methods employed in previous research where verbalisations are collected as athletes engage
332	 in exercise to investigate cognition [e.g., 27,42]. All decision-making clips were projected onto
333	 a television screen positioned outside the viewing window of the environmental chamber,
334	 directly in front of the participant. An omnidirectional boundary microphone (Samson
335	 CM11B, Samson Technologies, New York, US) was attached to the cycle ergometer to collect
336	 verbal responses and was connected via a small port to a laptop located outside of the
337	 chamber.
338	 Panopto software (Panopto 2020, Pittsburgh, US) was used to sync the video footage which
339	 was played from the laptop outside of the chamber, to the verbalised reports. Each recording
340	PLOS ONE | https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0279109 December 15, 2022 7 / 24
341	 PLOS ONE Exercise-induced fatigue and heat on soccer-specific decision-making during exercise
342	 was then downloaded as an MP4 file and transcribed ready for analysis in NVivo (QSR Inter-
343	 national 2020, Massachusetts, US). Inductive content analysis was used to analyse the record-
344	 ings obtained from the participants [42,43], allowing themes to emerge from the raw data as
345	 no similar research had been undertaken in soccer players to base pre-existing themes on.
346	 Firstly, verbalisations were coded openly where inductive themes continued to be generated
347	 from the raw data throughout the content analysis process. These codes were then categorised
348	 into themes and underlying sub-themes (See Table 2). The number of verbalisations for each
349	 theme and sub-theme was identified for each participant across the temperature conditions in
350	 NVivo and then recorded in Excel (Version 2008, Microsoft).
351	 Challenge and threat states. To assess challenge and threat states, demand and resource
352	 evaluations were measured to determine a cognitive appraisal ratio [44] pre-CISP and every
353	 3rd, 9th, 15th and 21st sprint in each half. At rest, participants were asked “How demanding do
354	 you expect the protocol to be?” and “How able are you to cope with the demands of the proto-
355	 col?” to measure demand evaluations and resource evaluations, respectively. The tense of these
356	 questions was then adapted for during the CISP (e.g., “How demanding are you finding the
357	 protocol?”). These two items were ranked using a 6-point Likert scale anchored from 1 (not at
358	 all) to 6 (extremely). A ratio was calculated by dividing demands by resources, where a value
359	 greater than 1 indicated a threat state, and less than 1 indicated a challenge state [44].
360	 Affect. Affective valence and activation were measured pre-CISP and every 3rd, 9th, 15th
361	 and 21st sprint of each half of the CISP using the Feeling Scale [45] anchored from -5 (very
362	 bad) through 0 (neutral) to 5 (very good). Unick et al. [46] also found excellent agreement dur-
363	 ing exercise within individuals across three sessions for the Feeling Scale (ICC = 0.83).
364	 Plasma metanephrines. For measurement of plasma metanephrines, 3ml blood samples
365	 were collected in ethylenediamine tetraacetic acid (EDTA) tubes from an indwelling venous
366	 catheter located in the arm at pre-CISP, half-time, and immediately post-CISP. These were
367	 centrifuged immediately (ALC; PK120R) and plasma separated for analysis of plasma metadre-
368	 naline (MET) and normetanephrine (NMET), measured as the more stable metabolites of
369	 plasma epinephrine and norepinephrine, respectively [47]. These samples were frozen at -80˚c
370	 until analysis by liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry in the Integrated Labora-
371	 tory Medicine Department, Freeman Hospital.
372	 Additional measures
373	 Core temperature (TC). TC was measured using a temperature sensor telemetry system in
374	 the form of a small ingestible pill. Participants ingested the thermometer pill ~6 hours prior to
375	 exercise [48]. TC was first recorded pre-trial following 15-min of seated rest to allow resting
376	 values to stabilise. TC was then recorded 1-min into each 2-min block, allowing a period for
377	 TC to stabilise following the 5-s sprint [39], and was also recorded this regularly for participant
378	 safety reasons. The TC recordings were averaged across 5-time points for each half of the CISP
379	 (i.e., every 10-min and the last 6-min of each 46-min half) for analysis.
380	 Heart rate. After sitting for 15-min to allow resting values to stabilise, participants HR
381	 (beats per min) was recorded using a polar HR monitor (FT1, Polar, Finland). HR was then
382	 recorded immediately after every sprint throughout the CISP, then averaged across 5-time
383	 points for each half of the CISP (i.e., every 10-min and the last-6-min of each 46-min half) for
384	 analysis.

386	 a secure room, undress, and step onto the Tanita scales to measure nude body mass immedi-
387	 ately pre- and post-each CISP, to determine fluid loss from the trial [49]. Urine osmolality was
388	 also measured immediately prior to nude body mass pre-CISP, where participants were asked

393	 time following the nude body mass procedure as per previous research [50], due to needing to

396	 sprint in each half of the CISP using Toner et al.’s [51] 0 (unbearably cold) to 8 (unbearably
397	 hot) Likert scale. This thermal sensation scale has been shown to be a valid measure of per-
398	 ceived heat stress, where correlations with large effect sizes (r = .72) have been shown between
399	 thermal sensation ratings and rectal temperature [52].

405	 Data analysis
406	 Statistical analysis was completed using IBM SPSS statistics 24.0 (IBM Corporation). After
407	 data screening and checking for normality of the data, a series of two-way (experimental con-
408	 dition by time) repeated measures ANOVAs were performed. Firstly, to analyse differences in
409	 indicators of physiological (e.g., core temperature, heart rate, fluid loss) and perceived psycho-
410	 logical (e.g., thermal sensation, RPE) strain. This was to check whether participants were
411	 under greater strain in the hot compared to the temperate condition. Then, a series of two-way
412	 repeated measures ANOVAs were performed to address our hypotheses. Specifically, to exam-

414	 ceived challenge and threat appraisals, affective valence, and plasma metanephrines.

416	 of variance was unable to be assumed, Greenhouse-Geisser corrections were applied. Where
417	 significant results were identified, Bonferroni pairwise comparisons post-hoc tests were per-
418	 formed. Two-tailed statistical significance was accepted at p � 0.05. All data were reported as
419	 means and standard deviation (SD). For visual clarity, Figure error bars represent standard
420	 error mean (SEM).

422	 ANOVAs. Due to Cohen’s [54] original partial eta-squared benchmarks of .01, .06 and .14 for
423	 small, medium, and large effects, respectively, not being suitable for interpreting partial eta-
424	 squared for multi-factorial within-subjects designs [55], these benchmarks were compared to
425	 generalized eta-squared which address considerations for which these benchmarks were based
426	 [55]. Additionally, Cohen’s d was reported as the effect size for pairwise comparisons. In accor-
427	 dance with Cohen [56], d values of 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 indicated small, moderate, and large effects
