260	Statistics and data analysis
261	Based on previous results for kicking accuracy, where participants kicked from 11 m,
262	similar outcomes were expected. However, due to the participants in our study not
263	immediately performing kicks after the fatigue protocol, the expected effect size was
264	anticipated to be half as large as Ferraz et al (R. M. P. Ferraz et al., 2019). The standard
265	deviation was assumed to be identical to the one from Russell, Benton (Russell et al.,
266	2011), which was 0.16 m. With a significance level set to 5%, this resulted in an estimated
267	requirement of 20 participants being included in the study to obtain the desired power of
268	80%. Based on these assumptions the final study population achieved in this study
269	(sixteen), yielded a calculated power of 65% for the accuracy outcome. For these
270	calculations StataBE-17, StataCorp LLC, USA was used.
271	 The torque values obtained from the dynamometer were analysed using Matlab
272	R2021a, MathWorks, USA. The maximum value (baseline subtracted) recorded during
273	each contraction was included for statistical data analysis across all measurements. An
274	example of the data from the intervention day for a participant is presented below

277	performance, StataBE-17, StataCorp LLC, USA was used. The results were compared
278	using paired t-tests, with a significance level of 5%. Regarding the intervention condition,
279	muscle fatigue comparisons of pre, post and end condition were analysed using one-way

281	were calculated by subtracting the individual pre- and post-data for each condition
282	(control and intervention) and comparing them. Assumptions of normality were checked

290	Seventeen experienced male soccer players (age 24.6 ± 2.1 years) ranging from amateur
291	(Serie1) to professional (Danish Superliga) level participated in the study. The groups
292	completed all tests during the test days, with one dropout in group 2 after the
293	introduction day due to an ankle injury unrelated to the current study. The results
294	from the test days were initially analysed separately for each group, and revealed no
295	sequence effects of the experimental protocol and the effect over time was not different

297	vention in both groups were pooled and compared to the pooled control days. The results

403	Discussion and implication
404	This study examines the effect of fatiguing muscle contractions on kicking perfor­
405	mance among experienced soccer players. After a fatigue protocol resulting in leg
406	extension MVIC fatigue and sustained LFF a reduction was found in maximum ball-
407	and foot speed from an instep kick, with no changes in maximum kicking accuracy.
408	However, in the control condition an increase in kick accuracy was found with no
409	effect on maximum foot or ball speed. Therefore, the effect of the intervention
410	appeared to be an absence of improvement in kicking accuracy following the fatigue
411	protocol. Therefore, our hypothesis was partly supported. The study highlights the
412	effect of more sustained fatigue, in this study LFF, on kicking in football since we
413	employed a standardised fatigue protocol while using direct measures of fatigue. The
414	  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS 13
415	fatigue protocol elicited fatigue in m. Quadriceps somewhat similar to the fatigue
416	experienced after a soccer match with a 14% reduction in MVIC peak force and high
417	frequency- low frequency stimulation ratio (Rampinini et al., 2011). Most studies
418	report a similar reduction in MVIC around 10% (3–14%) (Silva et al., 2018) examined
419	after a soccer match with some studies finding even greater MVIC deficits at 12.7% at
420	halftime and 18.5% at game end (Robineau et al., 2012), leaving the present reduction
421	in MVIC in the range of post-match fatigue. Regarding low frequency fatigue
422	Rampinini et al. (2011) reported a reduction in low frequency stimulation (10 hz)
423	force production of 9% with no significant change in high frequency stimulation
424	(100 hz) force production after a soccer match. Reduction in force production during
425	low firing rates is relevant to human voluntary muscle activation as the majority of
426	motor unit firing rates during MVIC ranges from 10-20 hz with a mean firing rate of
427	25 hz (Kirk & Rice, 2017). Muscle activation patterns of the quadriceps muscle during
428	an instep soccer kick does not seem to differ much from average MVIC EMG values
429	(Cerrah et al., 2011). Considering these similarities, we expected an effect of this type
430	of muscle fatigue on soccer kicking performance.
431	 In our study, the maximum kicking speed decreased by 1.9% following the fatigue
432	protocol. Similar fatigue-induced reductions between 0% and 5% are reported in pre­
433	vious studies (R. Ferraz et al., 2017; Radman, Wessner, Bachl, Ruzic, Hackl, Prpic, et al.,
434	2016; Rodríguez-Lorenzo et al., 2016; Russell et al., 2011; Torreblanca-Martínez et al.,
435	2020). Apriantono, Nunome (Apriantono et al., 2006), used a fatigue protocol performed
436	in a dynamometer targeting both knee extensors and flexors but with a lower intensity
437	than the present study. They found an acute decrease of 5.6% in maximum kicking speed
438	following fatigue. The acute nature of the test (<1 min of rest) likely contributed to
439	a larger decrease in kicking speed compared to the present study (1.9 %) which was
440	measured 30 minutes after the fatigue protocol. Further, Apriantono et al. (2006)
441	reported a significant relationship between foot speed and ball speed in the fresh state
442	which disappeared after performing muscle fatiguing work, consistent with other studies
443	(Levanon & Dapena, 1998; Nunome et al., 2006). Such a result indicates a decrease in the
444	variance in ball speed explained by foot speed. The reduced maximum ball speed in our
445	study appears to occur simultaneously with a numerical decrease in maximum foot speed
446	just before ball contact.
447	 In our study it is assumed that the decrease in maximum foot speed during the kick
448	explains the decrease in maximum ball speed. This is supported by the fact that the ball
449	speed/foot speed ratio did not significantly change on the intervention day compared to
450	the control day (−0,011 CI= [−0,086;0,064] p = 0.75). The results are based on the
451	maximal trial from the participants and therefore limit the conclusions to successful
452	trials in fatigued state.
453	 The present study utilised direct measures of decline in muscle performance (torque)
454	when investigating the effect of muscle fatigue on kicking accuracy. Many studies do not
455	measure muscle performance directly before and after a fatigue protocol and therefore do
456	not know whether or to what degree the participants are fatigued during the following
457	tests of kicking performance (Bjelica et al., 2013; R. Ferraz et al., 2017; Kellis et al., 2006;
458	Russell et al., 2011; W. Young et al., 2010). However, Torreblanca-Martínez et al. (2020)
459	did use direct measures of fatigue (decrease in sprint performance) and found a 5.67%
460	reduction on ball speed and a non-significant decrease in kicking accuracy of 7.69%.
461	 14 J. B. CARSTENSEN ET AL.
462	Despite a numerical decrease in players’ kicking accuracy, no significant results are found
463	due to large variation compared to ball speed (Katis et al., 2013; Radman, Wessner, Bachl,
464	Ruzic, Hackl, Prpic, et al., 2016). These findings are similar to the results of the present
465	study. However, Torreblanca-Martínez et al. (2020) did not include a control group for
466	comparison of kicking performance. Hence, limiting the possibility to detect the true
467	effect of the fatigue protocol as the none-fatigued condition could differ from a no-
468	change effect. This is supported by the findings of the present study and Currell et al.
469	(2009) who found a significant improvement in shooting performance in their interven­
470	tion compared with placebo. The present study showed an improvement in kicking
471	accuracy on the control day of 13.3% (p = 0.02). Despite this conclusion, the significant
472	improvement observed on the control day still comes as a surprise to us and is to our
473	knowledge not observed before perhaps due to the lack of control conditions in many
474	studies. Given the high level among the study participants, the standardised warm-up
475	protocol, and the uncomplicated test protocol, we did not anticipate any change on the
476	control day. Nevertheless, this unexpected outcome occurred hence, demonstrating the
477	importance of including a control group in tests where an effect over time is not expected.
478	 In studies by Ferraz et al. (2019) and Russell et al. (2011) a combination of direct and
479	indirect measures of muscle fatigue was used. Analogous to our study, the studies do not
480	find decreases in kicking accuracy. The studies used a decrease in running performance,
481	heart rate, and perceived exertion on the Borg scale. The results from these studies show
482	that heart rate and perceived fatigue increase, while the direct measures (running
483	performance) do not change (R. M. P. Ferraz et al., 2019; Russell et al., 2011).
484	Therefore, it is uncertain whether the participants actually experienced muscle fatigue
485	in these studies, which could potentially explain why kicking accuracy was not affected.
486	 The distribution of kicks from the participants in the accuracy test was described using
487	bivariate normal distribution and showed similar characteristics to the results from
488	Hunter et al. (2018). Accordingly, the effect of the fatiguing muscle contractions was
489	an increased short axis on the error ellipse describing the distribution of the kicks. This is
490	thought to be due to a disturbance in the timing of muscle activation in the kicking
491	motion caused by the effect of fatigue on contractile properties in the involved muscu­
492	lature. When kicking a rolling ball this disturbance in timing may have resulted in
493	a larger variance in the distance between support leg placement and ball in the moment
494	of contact with the kicking leg.
495	Role of the quadriceps muscle
496	The type of fatigue that we have induced in the present study, LFF, seems to primarily
497	decrease the muscle’s ability to develop force during slow or static contractions
498	without the same diminishing effect on maximum contraction velocity (Herskind,
499	2022; Herskind et al., 2022). This influence on the force-velocity curve of muscles
500	exposed to LFF possibly affects intersegmental coordination during complex multi-
501	joint movements like the instep kick. However, it should be noted that there is limited
502	data on the effect of LFF on muscle contractions near maximum contraction velocity,
503	and conclusions based on these data should be cautious (Herskind, 2022). Therefore,
504	if the force velocity relationship of the m. quadriceps is affected during fatigue kicking
505	conditions reducing timing of muscle activation and intersegmental coordination this
506	  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS 15
507	would cause a reduction in maximal foot- and ball speed as observed in the present
508	study.
509	 In a review by Young and Rath (2011), the authors discuss that resistance exercise
510	induced increase in maximum kicking speed among soccer players is not achieved by
511	targeting isolated parts of the kicking movement, e.g., the quadriceps muscle
512	(W. B. Young & Rath, 2011). Based on this reasoning, it could be speculated that
513	the opposite scenario is true; isolated fatigue in the quadriceps femoris muscle of the
514	kicking leg would not affect maximum kicking speed. The results of the present study
515	do however contradict this, as we show that performing an instep kick in a fatigued
516	state (fatigued quadriceps muscle of kicking leg) does reduce maximum kicking
517	speed. It should be noted though, that the review by Young and Rath (2011) primarily
518	focuses on ankle speed immediately before ball contact. Results from the
519	intervention day showed a 5.86% (p = 0.035) decrease in maximum foot speed in
520	fatigued state and a trend observed in the between day difference of 6.3% (p = 0.054).
521	The ambiguity of these results in the literature initiates a discussion on the role of
522	knee extensors during a soccer kick. In a 2010 review, Lees et al. (2010) conclude that
523	the angular velocities of the knee (860–1720 degrees per second) (Kellis & Katis,
524	2007) result in such high contraction velocities for the quadriceps femoris muscle that
525	ankle-accelerating work from this muscle must be extremely limited. The authors also
526	conclude that hip flexors are the prime movers in the movement, and the majority of
527	knee extensor torque comes from thigh angular velocity during the movement (Dörge
528	et al., 2002; Kellis & Katis, 2007; Kellis et al., 2006; Lees et al., 2010). Therefore,
529	a fatigue protocol that affects the iliopsoas muscle could be an interesting extension of
530	the study. These findings also highlight the importance of intersegmental coordina­
531	tion during the movement, as emphasised by the differences observed in the kinetics
532	and kinematics between soccer players’ preferred and non-preferred legs (Dörge et al.,
533	2002; Nunome et al., 2006). These kinematic differences, such as increased resulting
534	ball speed and foot speed for the preferred leg, are not due to differences in muscle
535	strength between the legs but are kinetically attributed to increased work on the lower
536	leg resulting from interaction torque through greater thigh angular velocity and
537	a greater relative knee extensor muscle torque (Dörge et al., 2002; Nunome et al.,
538	2006). Similarly, Apriantono et al. (2006) reported that muscle fatigue reduced this
539	interaction torque acting on the proximal end of the lower leg as well as knee joint
540	torque. These are probably not the only contributing factors affecting the resulting
541	foot- and ankle speed. Another possible factor affected by the muscle could be the
542	run-up speed before ball impact which was not measured in this study. Is the run-up
543	speed slower due to muscle fatigue, this would result in less deceleration of the centre
544	of mass before ball contact and therefore less impulse to be transferred to the foot
545	(Potthast et al., 2010). This could possibly result in lower maximal foot and ankle
546	speed.The fact that ball speed and foot speed before ball contact are reduced in
547	relation to fatigue of the quadriceps femoris muscle in this study suggests
548	a disruption in intersegmental coordination during the soccer kick, which may be
549	caused by altered contraction dynamics disturbing the timing of muscle activation
550	due to muscle fatigue (Herskind et al., 2022).
551	 16 J. B. CARSTENSEN ET AL.
552	Methodological considerations
553	The sample size of the present study was based on a sample size predicting a need for 20
554	included participants. However, only 16 individuals completed this study hence the
555	findings of the present study might be prone to type two errors.
556	 Kicking accuracy was measured in kicks with a requirement of ≥ 80% individual
557	maximum kicking speed as kicking accuracy decreases as the speed requirement
558	increases (Andersen & Dörge, 2011; Hunter et al., 2018).
559	 The methodological approach resulted in the exclusion of kicks falling below this
560	threshold. We did not systematically analyse or count the excluded kicks in all partici­
561	pants. However, if the number of kicks below the speed-criterium is influenced, this
562	outcome may represent valuable additional information for future studies.
563	Perspectives and practical applications
564	The results from this study indicate that maximal kicking speed is reduced with muscle
565	fatigue and kicking distribution is altered with an increased error ellipse shorts axis.
566	A possible effect of this is a reduced chance on goal scoring on a given kick late in the
567	game when players experience muscle fatigue.
568	 A goalkeeper’s reach is determined by the speed of the kick when taken from the penalty
569	spot. A given goalkeeper’s maximal take-off velocity is constant, and the variable in the
570	situation is the time it takes for the ball to travel after being kicked from the kicker’s foot
571	determining the time for the goalkeeper to travel after taking off from the ground. The faster
572	the ball travels, the less time the goalkeeper can travel before the ball passes by and enters the
573	goal. On the intervention day during the accuracy measurements, the players kicked on
574	average 27.88 m/s ±1.16 m/s before fatigue and 27.44 m/s ±1.37 m/s after fatigue, providing
575	the goalkeeper with an additional 0.0064s (1.6%) to react to the kick. The increased reaction
576	time may extend the goalkeeper’s reach during the kick and hence reduces the chance of goal
577	scoring. The decrease in average ball speed during the accuracy test although not statistically
578	significant followed the decrease in maximal ball speed of 1.9% corresponding to equal effort
579	levels during the tests. On the control day average ball speed during the accuracy test did not
580	change statistically but increased numerically from 27,69 m/s ±1.21 m/s to 27.92 m/s ±1.09
581	m/s an increase of 0.8% following a similar small non-significant increase of 0.2% in the
582	maximal ball speed test again corresponding to equal effort levels during these tests.
583	 Furthermore, the increased error ellipse describing the dispersion pattern of kicks could
584	bring about changes in the proportion of kicks ending up in the ‘scoring zone’ (inside the
585	goal but outside the reach of the goalkeeper). The areas of the dispersion ellipses were not
586	significantly altered after fatigue in the present study. Therefore, the effect of muscle fatigue
587	would be the altered shape of the error ellipse. Depending on the aiming point this more
588	elongated error ellipse possibly results in a reduced number of shots ending up in the
589	‘scoring zone’ or alter the optimal point of aim more centrally in the goal.
590	Conclusion
591	The findings of the present study showed a reduction in the players’ maximum kicking
592	speed following a fatigue inducing protocol of the quadriceps femoris muscle. A decrease
593	  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS 17
594	in maximum foot speed immediately before ball contact is likely the cause of the lowered
595	maximum kicking speed. The effect on kicking accuracy is not conclusive due to greater
596	data variation and a lack of statistical power in the study. However, an improved kicking
597	accuracy was observed on the control day, but not on the day of the fatigue intervention.
598	The implications of muscle-fatiguing work on kicking skills are, however, not definitively
599	described in this study and require further research.

Introduction
Soccer is the largest and most popular sport in the world (Lovett, 2018). Crucial to the
outcome of a soccer match is the ability to score goals. The soccer kick has been
extensively studied as a crucial element in this regard (Barfield et al., 2002). Two
important components of a well-performed kick are ball speed and the accuracy with
which a player is able to place the ball (Dörge et al., 2002; Katis et al., 2013; Lees & Nolan,
1998). The ability to achieve high speed and accuracy in soccer kicks may be influenced
by muscle fatigue as the physical demands of soccer are characterised by intermittent
high-intensity work (Bangsbo, 2014; Bangsbo et al., 2006). This intermittent work leads
to both momentary fatigue during a match due to high-intensity periods as well as
gradual accumulation of fatigue towards the end of the game (Dambroz et al., 2022).

 2 J. B. CARSTENSEN ET AL.
 Muscle fatigue is defined by Allen, Lamb referred to as prolonged low frequency
force depression or low-frequency fatigue (LFF). LFF is a phenomenon charac­
terised by a greater decrease in muscle force production when tested at low
stimulation frequencies compared to high stimulation frequencies after fatiguing
muscle contractions (Keeton & Binder-Macleod, 2006). Furthermore, recovery of
muscle performance is slow from LFF, and typically ranges from a few hours to
several days (De Ruiter et al., 2005; Edwards et al., 1977; Jones et al., 1989). The
primary cause of LFF is a reduced release of Ca++ from the sarcoplasmic reticulum
(Allen et al., 2008). In humans LFF elicits deficits in both force and power during
dynamic contraction (Herskind et al., 2023). In a soccer context, LFF has been
demonstrated to be present during post-match recovery expressed as reduced 10 hz/
100 hz muscle stimulation force ratio (Rampinini et al., 2011). Although fatigue of
more temporary character is also present after intense periods during soccer
matches (Mohr et al., 2005) we have focussed particularly on the more long-
lasting LFF in the present study.
 In experiments based on multi-joint movements, Forestier and Nougier (1998) exam­
ined the effect of muscle fatigue in the wrist flexor muscles on coordination and accuracy
of seated throwing. Fatigue, induced by isometric contractions of the wrist flexor,
reduced the proportion of accurate throws from 77% to 57%. This reduced accuracy
occurred concomitantly with changes in throwing mechanics from a successive prox­
imal-to-distal accelerating movement to a more simultaneous movement of joint systems
(shoulder, elbow, and wrist) displaying increased rigidity (Forestier & Nougier, 1998).
These results are interesting in a soccer context as soccer kicks in a fresh state follow
similar movement characteristics as throwing (Kellis & Katis, 2007). Whether changing
kinematics due to fatigue are also present during a maximal soccer kick is uncertain.
 The literature on soccer kicks indicates that maximal kick speed and foot speed before
ball contact are reduced in the fatigued state immediately after intense activity
(Apriantono et al., 2006; R. Ferraz et al., 2012; R. M. P. Ferraz et al., 2019; Kellis et al.,
2006; Torreblanca-Martínez et al., 2020). However, due to lack of objective assessments
of muscle fatigue, the level of fatigue among the participants in these studies is uncertain.
Some discrepancy is observed in the effect of fatigue on kicking accuracy. Thus,
Torreblanca-Martínez et al. (2020) found no change in kicking accuracy after sprint
work while Bjelica et al. (2013) found a decrease in soccer players’ kicking accuracy
kicking at different intensities (self-selected or maximum) when performed in a fatigued
state. In line with this, Stone and Oliver (2009) found a decrease in points scored in the
Loughborough Soccer Shooting Test (LSST) after 45 minutes of soccer-like interval-
based muscle work, accompanied by an 85% increase in kicks resulting in 0 points
(worst outcome of a kick).
 Kicking accuracy is often measured by the LSST which divides the football goal
into scoring zones (Alkhawaldeh, 2022; Engler et al., 2023; Gardasevic & Bjelica,
2019; Islam et al., 2019; Stone & Oliver, 2009; Torreblanca-Martínez et al., 2020).
The test is argued to be valid and does also discriminate between groups with
expected differences in skill level (Ali et al., 2007). However, the test is limited by
a high complexity, low spatial resolution of scoring zones, and participants’ risk
willingness as scoring zones with high points and zones with low points are
adjacent (Dambroz et al., 2022). To eliminate this methodological issue a simpler
  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS 3
‘distance to target’ kick-test is proposed to measure kicking accuracy (Bjelica et al.,
2013; R. M. P. Ferraz et al., 2019; Finnoff et al., 2002; Radman, Wessner, Bachl,
Ruzic, Hackl, Baca, et al., 2016).
 Examining the effect of muscle fatigue in this context poses further challenges. These
include the rapid recovery of acute muscle fatigue after running or soccer match
simulation. Therefore, the results from such protocols are highly dependent on the
time interval between the fatigue protocol and the test protocol (Bjelica et al., 2013;
Dambroz et al., 2022; R. M. P. Ferraz et al., 2019; Russell et al., 2011; Torreblanca-
Martínez et al., 2020). Another problem arises from the fact that indirect measures of
fatigue are diverse and could include central cardiovascular parameters such as heart rate
(R. Ferraz et al., 2012, 2017; Kellis et al., 2006; Radman, Wessner, Bachl, Ruzic, Hackl,
Prpic, et al., 2016; Russell et al., 2011; Stone & Oliver, 2009), perceived exertion (RPE) on
the Borg scale (R. Ferraz et al., 2012, 2017; R. M. P. Ferraz et al., 2019; Radman, Wessner,
Bachl, Ruzic, Hackl, Prpic, et al., 2016; Russell et al., 2011), or surrogate measures such as
blood lactate concentration (R. Ferraz et al., 2012, 2017; R. M. P. Ferraz et al., 2019; Kellis
et al., 2006; Radman, Wessner, Bachl, Ruzic, Hackl, Prpic, et al., 2016; Russell et al., 2011).
None of these parameters directly refer to Allen and Lamb’s definition of muscle fatigue
(Allen et al., 2008) and only RPE has been shown to yield a negative correlation with
kicking accuracy (Torreblanca-Martínez et al., 2020; Vøllestad, 1997). To eliminate issues
regarding the time sensitive nature of acute muscle fatigue and to align with the defini­
tion of muscle fatigue (Allen et al., 2008), measuring maximal voluntary isometric
contraction force (MVIC) and force induced by electrical stimulation with high or low
frequency after performing a fatigue protocol would be advantageous. LFF has a long
duration and is relatively stable during the first hour after a fatigue protocol when soccer
tests are completed (Keeton & Binder-Macleod, 2006; Sieljacks et al., 2015).
 The purpose of the present study was to clarify the effect of muscle fatigue on kick
performance among skilled soccer players. The hypothesis was that a fatiguing protocol
inducing LFF and decreased MVIC would lead to a reduction in maximum ball speed,
maximum foot speed, and kicking accuracy of the soccer players.
Materials and methods
Study design
The present study is a randomised controlled crossover trial comparing the effects of
a fatigue protocol on soccer kick performance to a control condition (rest). Group 1 (n =
9) received the fatiguing protocol on the first trial day and then the control condition
separated by one week. Group 2 (n = 7) received the control condition first and then the
fatiguing protocol separated by one week (see Figure 1 for illustration of study design and
testing). At a visit three days prior to the first trial day, participants were familiarised with
tests in the dynamometer and electrical stimulation.
 The study was conducted in accordance with ethical research guidelines and partici­
pation was voluntary and was consented to by all participants after written and oral
information of the study procedures was provided. Full consideration for ethical
approval was, however, waived by the regional committee for research ethics (reference
number 1-10-72-124-22) as the study was not considered as biomedical research.
 4 J. B. CARSTENSEN ET AL.
Figure 1. Overview of the experimental design and test protocol.
Participants
Seventeen experienced male soccer players ranging from high-ranking amateur (Serie1) to
professional (Danish Superliga) level were recruited directly through the authors’ network,
advertisements in soccer clubs, and social media postings and were randomised into two
groups. Group 2 experienced one dropout after the introduction day due to an ankle injury
unrelated to the current study. To be eligible for inclusion participants had to be active male
soccer players aged 18–30 years with a minimum of 10 years of experience of playing
organised soccer (Apriantono et al., 2006), and currently play at a Serie1 level or higher.
Further, participants were encouraged to refrain from physical activity 48 hours before
testing. Descriptive characteristics of the participants are presented in Table 1.
Table 1. Descriptive characteristics of the participants. Data are presented as mean ± SD. Groups were
pooled as no differences in characteristics were found between the two groups.
 N Age (years) Height (cm) weight (kg) Experience (years)
 Participants 16 24.6 � 2.1 184,5 � 5.7 80.3 � 5.8 19.8 � 2.2
Dynamometric assessment of voluntary and electrically induced contractions of
the kicking leg
Participants were positioned in the isokinetic dynamometer to perform knee extension.
Two 5 × 10 cm electrodes (Valutrode Lite, Axelgaard, Denmark) were placed on shaved
and disinfected skin over the quadriceps muscle 15 cm above the basis of the patella and
15 cm below the anterior superior iliac crest based on the methods described by
Gaemelke et al. (2021). The axis of rotation of the dynamometer was aligned with the
knee, participants were secured with shoulder and hip harnesses, and range of motion of
each participant was set for knee extension and flexion.
 MVIC of the knee extensors was measured at a 70° knee angle (where 0 represents full
knee extension) due to peak torque being greatest at around this knee angle (Pincivero
et al., 2004). The hip angle was 80° (where 0° represents full hip extension). Participants
were instructed to contract their muscles as quickly and forcefully as possible, and to
maintain this contraction for 2–3 seconds while standardised strong verbal motivation
was provided. MVIC was measured three times on the intervention day and two times on
  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS 5
the control day. After the MVIC measurement, the participants had a 2-minute rest
period before the electric stimulation protocol.
 LFF was measured using electrical stimulation. The participants were instructed to relax
as much as possible before and during the stimulation. Stimulation was delivered at 125
mA with a pulse width of 0.2 ms and a train duration of 0.8s at 15 hz and 50 hz based on
results from Edwards et al. (1977). The participants had a 1-minute rest period between the
stimulations (Sieljacks et al., 2015). Torque data was sampled at 1500 hz and LFF was
calculated as the ratio between maximal torque at 15 hz stimulation and 50 hz stimulation.
Fatigue protocol
The fatigue protocol was performed with the kicking leg and consisted of maximal
voluntary isokinetic knee extensor actions performed at 60°/s both concentrically and
eccentrically as controlled by the dynamometer (Humac Norm, CSMi, Stoughton, MA).
One repetition was regarded as a concentric contraction of the knee extensors followed
by an eccentric contraction of the knee extensors. Range of motion (ROM) was defined
from 5° below maximal knee flexion angle to 5° before maximal knee extension.
Participants typically had ROM of 95° corresponding to knee flexion angle 5° to 100°.
One repetition lasted approximately 3 seconds and participants were given no rest
between repetitions. A total of 5 sets of 10 consecutive repetitions with a 10-second inter-
set rest period were performed. Participants were instructed to exert maximal effort and
were provided with standardised verbal encouragement and visual feedback of their force
trace on a screen. This protocol was chosen as it has previously been shown to induce LFF
(Herskind et al., 2023). After the fatigue protocol participants had a 3-minute rest period
before the subsequent dynamometric testing.
Kicking performance
Kicking performance was measured on the dominant leg only. Testing was performed in
an indoor biomechanical laboratory with artificial grass floor using a Select Brilliant
Super ball inflated to 0.9 bar. Participants used their regular soccer boots and were asked
to use the same pair for both test days due to results from Sterzing and Hennig (2008).
Prior to testing, participants performed a standardised warm-up consisting of 5 minutes
of self-selected intensity cycling, 20 leg swings with the kicking leg (10 in the sagittal axis
and 10 in the transverse axis), and 3 warm-up kicks at self-selected intensity.
 Maximum ball speed was measured using a Supido Sports Speed Radar during three
kicks on a stationary ball at distance of 11 metres, emulating a penalty kick. The speed
radar was placed directly behind a kicking target suspended in a net. The participants
were instructed to kick with maximal force using the instep kick and rested 30 seconds
between kicks. The hardest kick (ball speed) was used for data analysis of all kicking
performance variables. If a player improved through all 3 kicks, additional attempts were
given until the improvement ceased.
 Maximum foot speed was measured using a laser system just before ball contact. Two
lasers placed 3 cm apart in the kicking direction recording the time between the foot
intersecting laser 1 to laser 2 yielding the speed of the foot in the final swing phase. This
measurement was obtained during the maximal ball speed test.

 Kicking accuracy was measured using a two-camera system determining distance
from ball impact to target (a cross suspended at 1.22 metres) (R. M. P. Ferraz et al.,
2019). A total of 10 kicks were performed from 11 m with 30 s rest periods between kicks
(Radman, Wessner, Bachl, Ruzic, Hackl, Baca, et al., 2016). Similarly to Radman,
Wessner, Bachl, Ruzic, Hackl, Baca, et al. (2016) the ball was rolled forward and kicked
while moving for this test. Based on results from (Andersen & Dörge, 2011; Hunter et al.,
2018), participants were instructed to kick at a minimum of 80% of their measured
current maximum speed. If a kick did not reach the required speed, the kick was
discarded from data analysis and the player performed a new attempt. Ball speed was
measured using the speed radar as in the maximal ball speed test. The two-camera system
consisted of two recording wall mounted cameras (Brio 4K Ultra HD Webcam, Logitech)
spanning the field in the plane of the target cross perpendicular to the kicking direction
(Figure 2). The position of ball impact was determined by triangulation using pixel values
from the two cameras. The Euclidian distance between ball impact and target cross was
then determined and used for analysis. The analyses were performed using MatLab
R2021a, MathWorks, USA.

Distribution of kicks
To further analyse kicking accuracy, the kick dispersion was described using bivariate
distributions based on the results of Hunter (2018). A 95% CI error ellipse was obtained
from each participant from the trial days. Data from left footed kickers was mirrored and
pooled with data from right footed kickers. The results are described in Table 3 comparing
short axis, long axis, area, and angle of the error ellipse describing the kick distribution.

Statistics and data analysis
Based on previous results for kicking accuracy, where participants kicked from 11 m,
similar outcomes were expected. However, due to the participants in our study not
immediately performing kicks after the fatigue protocol, the expected effect size was
anticipated to be half as large as Ferraz et al (R. M. P. Ferraz et al., 2019). The standard
deviation was assumed to be identical to the one from Russell, Benton (Russell et al.,
2011), which was 0.16 m. With a significance level set to 5%, this resulted in an estimated
requirement of 20 participants being included in the study to obtain the desired power of
80%. Based on these assumptions the final study population achieved in this study
(sixteen), yielded a calculated power of 65% for the accuracy outcome. For these
calculations StataBE-17, StataCorp LLC, USA was used.
 The torque values obtained from the dynamometer were analysed using Matlab
R2021a, MathWorks, USA. The maximum value (baseline subtracted) recorded during
each contraction was included for statistical data analysis across all measurements. An
example of the data from the intervention day for a participant is presented below
(Figure 3).
 For statistical analysis of the contraction measurements and measurements of kicking
performance, StataBE-17, StataCorp LLC, USA was used. The results were compared
using paired t-tests, with a significance level of 5%. Regarding the intervention condition,
muscle fatigue comparisons of pre, post and end condition were analysed using one-way
repeated measures ANOVA with Bonferroni correction. The between group differences
were calculated by subtracting the individual pre- and post-data for each condition
(control and intervention) and comparing them. Assumptions of normality were checked
visually using qq-plots.

Results
Seventeen experienced male soccer players (age 24.6 ± 2.1 years) ranging from amateur
(Serie1) to professional (Danish Superliga) level participated in the study. The groups
completed all tests during the test days, with one dropout in group 2 after the
introduction day due to an ankle injury unrelated to the current study. The results
from the test days were initially analysed separately for each group, and revealed no
sequence effects of the experimental protocol and the effect over time was not different
between the groups (not shown). Therefore, the measurements from the fatigue inter­
vention in both groups were pooled and compared to the pooled control days. The results
of the kicking performance tests from the two conditions are presented in Tables 2 and 3.
Muscle fatigue tests
MVIC measurements are illustrated in Figure 4. On the intervention day, a decrease in
MVIC of 14.0% (CI = [8.7%; 19.4%], p < 0.01) was observed following the fatigue protocol.
After the post-kicking measurements (MVIC end), the decrease was 13.5% (CI = [7.0%;
19.9%], p < 0.01) compared to the pre-value. There was no difference between the post-
measurement and end-measurement (p = 0.80) showing a stable degree of fatigue. On the
control day, the torque did not change at any time point, and the effect over time differed
from the intervention day (12.5% CI = [2.86%; 22.2%], p = 0.015).
 The results from the electrical stimulation are illustrated in Figures 5 and 6. We did
not perform any specific measurements to ascertain that all parts of the quadriceps
muscle were activated, However, we have used the present stimulation setup and
electrode configuration in previous studies, where we have observed that we are able to
obtain > 70% of maximal voluntary torque of knee extensors, indicating that a large part
of the quadriceps is activated during electrical stimulation (Gravholt et al., 2022).

Discussion and implication
This study examines the effect of fatiguing muscle contractions on kicking perfor­
mance among experienced soccer players. After a fatigue protocol resulting in leg
extension MVIC fatigue and sustained LFF a reduction was found in maximum ball-
and foot speed from an instep kick, with no changes in maximum kicking accuracy.
However, in the control condition an increase in kick accuracy was found with no
effect on maximum foot or ball speed. Therefore, the effect of the intervention
appeared to be an absence of improvement in kicking accuracy following the fatigue
protocol. Therefore, our hypothesis was partly supported. The study highlights the
effect of more sustained fatigue, in this study LFF, on kicking in football since we
employed a standardised fatigue protocol while using direct measures of fatigue. The
  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS 13
fatigue protocol elicited fatigue in m. Quadriceps somewhat similar to the fatigue
experienced after a soccer match with a 14% reduction in MVIC peak force and high
frequency- low frequency stimulation ratio (Rampinini et al., 2011). Most studies
report a similar reduction in MVIC around 10% (3–14%) (Silva et al., 2018) examined
after a soccer match with some studies finding even greater MVIC deficits at 12.7% at
halftime and 18.5% at game end (Robineau et al., 2012), leaving the present reduction
in MVIC in the range of post-match fatigue. Regarding low frequency fatigue
Rampinini et al. (2011) reported a reduction in low frequency stimulation (10 hz)
force production of 9% with no significant change in high frequency stimulation
(100 hz) force production after a soccer match. Reduction in force production during
low firing rates is relevant to human voluntary muscle activation as the majority of
motor unit firing rates during MVIC ranges from 10-20 hz with a mean firing rate of
25 hz (Kirk & Rice, 2017). Muscle activation patterns of the quadriceps muscle during
an instep soccer kick does not seem to differ much from average MVIC EMG values
(Cerrah et al., 2011). Considering these similarities, we expected an effect of this type
of muscle fatigue on soccer kicking performance.
 In our study, the maximum kicking speed decreased by 1.9% following the fatigue
protocol. Similar fatigue-induced reductions between 0% and 5% are reported in pre­
vious studies (R. Ferraz et al., 2017; Radman, Wessner, Bachl, Ruzic, Hackl, Prpic, et al.,
2016; Rodríguez-Lorenzo et al., 2016; Russell et al., 2011; Torreblanca-Martínez et al.,
2020). Apriantono, Nunome (Apriantono et al., 2006), used a fatigue protocol performed
in a dynamometer targeting both knee extensors and flexors but with a lower intensity
than the present study. They found an acute decrease of 5.6% in maximum kicking speed
following fatigue. The acute nature of the test (<1 min of rest) likely contributed to
a larger decrease in kicking speed compared to the present study (1.9 %) which was
measured 30 minutes after the fatigue protocol. Further, Apriantono et al. (2006)
reported a significant relationship between foot speed and ball speed in the fresh state
which disappeared after performing muscle fatiguing work, consistent with other studies
(Levanon & Dapena, 1998; Nunome et al., 2006). Such a result indicates a decrease in the
variance in ball speed explained by foot speed. The reduced maximum ball speed in our
study appears to occur simultaneously with a numerical decrease in maximum foot speed
just before ball contact.
 In our study it is assumed that the decrease in maximum foot speed during the kick
explains the decrease in maximum ball speed. This is supported by the fact that the ball
speed/foot speed ratio did not significantly change on the intervention day compared to
the control day (−0,011 CI= [−0,086;0,064] p = 0.75). The results are based on the
maximal trial from the participants and therefore limit the conclusions to successful
trials in fatigued state.
 The present study utilised direct measures of decline in muscle performance (torque)
when investigating the effect of muscle fatigue on kicking accuracy. Many studies do not
measure muscle performance directly before and after a fatigue protocol and therefore do
not know whether or to what degree the participants are fatigued during the following
tests of kicking performance (Bjelica et al., 2013; R. Ferraz et al., 2017; Kellis et al., 2006;
Russell et al., 2011; W. Young et al., 2010). However, Torreblanca-Martínez et al. (2020)
did use direct measures of fatigue (decrease in sprint performance) and found a 5.67%
reduction on ball speed and a non-significant decrease in kicking accuracy of 7.69%.
 14 J. B. CARSTENSEN ET AL.
Despite a numerical decrease in players’ kicking accuracy, no significant results are found
due to large variation compared to ball speed (Katis et al., 2013; Radman, Wessner, Bachl,
Ruzic, Hackl, Prpic, et al., 2016). These findings are similar to the results of the present
study. However, Torreblanca-Martínez et al. (2020) did not include a control group for
comparison of kicking performance. Hence, limiting the possibility to detect the true
effect of the fatigue protocol as the none-fatigued condition could differ from a no-
change effect. This is supported by the findings of the present study and Currell et al.
(2009) who found a significant improvement in shooting performance in their interven­
tion compared with placebo. The present study showed an improvement in kicking
accuracy on the control day of 13.3% (p = 0.02). Despite this conclusion, the significant
improvement observed on the control day still comes as a surprise to us and is to our
knowledge not observed before perhaps due to the lack of control conditions in many
studies. Given the high level among the study participants, the standardised warm-up
protocol, and the uncomplicated test protocol, we did not anticipate any change on the
control day. Nevertheless, this unexpected outcome occurred hence, demonstrating the
importance of including a control group in tests where an effect over time is not expected.
 In studies by Ferraz et al. (2019) and Russell et al. (2011) a combination of direct and
indirect measures of muscle fatigue was used. Analogous to our study, the studies do not
find decreases in kicking accuracy. The studies used a decrease in running performance,
heart rate, and perceived exertion on the Borg scale. The results from these studies show
that heart rate and perceived fatigue increase, while the direct measures (running
performance) do not change (R. M. P. Ferraz et al., 2019; Russell et al., 2011).
Therefore, it is uncertain whether the participants actually experienced muscle fatigue
in these studies, which could potentially explain why kicking accuracy was not affected.
 The distribution of kicks from the participants in the accuracy test was described using
bivariate normal distribution and showed similar characteristics to the results from
Hunter et al. (2018). Accordingly, the effect of the fatiguing muscle contractions was
an increased short axis on the error ellipse describing the distribution of the kicks. This is
thought to be due to a disturbance in the timing of muscle activation in the kicking
motion caused by the effect of fatigue on contractile properties in the involved muscu­
lature. When kicking a rolling ball this disturbance in timing may have resulted in
a larger variance in the distance between support leg placement and ball in the moment
of contact with the kicking leg.
Role of the quadriceps muscle
The type of fatigue that we have induced in the present study, LFF, seems to primarily
decrease the muscle’s ability to develop force during slow or static contractions
without the same diminishing effect on maximum contraction velocity (Herskind,
2022; Herskind et al., 2022). This influence on the force-velocity curve of muscles
exposed to LFF possibly affects intersegmental coordination during complex multi-
joint movements like the instep kick. However, it should be noted that there is limited
data on the effect of LFF on muscle contractions near maximum contraction velocity,
and conclusions based on these data should be cautious (Herskind, 2022). Therefore,
if the force velocity relationship of the m. quadriceps is affected during fatigue kicking
conditions reducing timing of muscle activation and intersegmental coordination this
  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS 15
would cause a reduction in maximal foot- and ball speed as observed in the present
study.
 In a review by Young and Rath (2011), the authors discuss that resistance exercise
induced increase in maximum kicking speed among soccer players is not achieved by
targeting isolated parts of the kicking movement, e.g., the quadriceps muscle
(W. B. Young & Rath, 2011). Based on this reasoning, it could be speculated that
the opposite scenario is true; isolated fatigue in the quadriceps femoris muscle of the
kicking leg would not affect maximum kicking speed. The results of the present study
do however contradict this, as we show that performing an instep kick in a fatigued
state (fatigued quadriceps muscle of kicking leg) does reduce maximum kicking
speed. It should be noted though, that the review by Young and Rath (2011) primarily
focuses on ankle speed immediately before ball contact. Results from the
intervention day showed a 5.86% (p = 0.035) decrease in maximum foot speed in
fatigued state and a trend observed in the between day difference of 6.3% (p = 0.054).
The ambiguity of these results in the literature initiates a discussion on the role of
knee extensors during a soccer kick. In a 2010 review, Lees et al. (2010) conclude that
the angular velocities of the knee (860–1720 degrees per second) (Kellis & Katis,
2007) result in such high contraction velocities for the quadriceps femoris muscle that
ankle-accelerating work from this muscle must be extremely limited. The authors also
conclude that hip flexors are the prime movers in the movement, and the majority of
knee extensor torque comes from thigh angular velocity during the movement (Dörge
et al., 2002; Kellis & Katis, 2007; Kellis et al., 2006; Lees et al., 2010). Therefore,
a fatigue protocol that affects the iliopsoas muscle could be an interesting extension of
the study. These findings also highlight the importance of intersegmental coordina­
tion during the movement, as emphasised by the differences observed in the kinetics
and kinematics between soccer players’ preferred and non-preferred legs (Dörge et al.,
2002; Nunome et al., 2006). These kinematic differences, such as increased resulting
ball speed and foot speed for the preferred leg, are not due to differences in muscle
strength between the legs but are kinetically attributed to increased work on the lower
leg resulting from interaction torque through greater thigh angular velocity and
a greater relative knee extensor muscle torque (Dörge et al., 2002; Nunome et al.,
2006). Similarly, Apriantono et al. (2006) reported that muscle fatigue reduced this
interaction torque acting on the proximal end of the lower leg as well as knee joint
torque. These are probably not the only contributing factors affecting the resulting
foot- and ankle speed. Another possible factor affected by the muscle could be the
run-up speed before ball impact which was not measured in this study. Is the run-up
speed slower due to muscle fatigue, this would result in less deceleration of the centre
of mass before ball contact and therefore less impulse to be transferred to the foot
(Potthast et al., 2010). This could possibly result in lower maximal foot and ankle
speed.The fact that ball speed and foot speed before ball contact are reduced in
relation to fatigue of the quadriceps femoris muscle in this study suggests
a disruption in intersegmental coordination during the soccer kick, which may be
caused by altered contraction dynamics disturbing the timing of muscle activation
due to muscle fatigue (Herskind et al., 2022).
 16 J. B. CARSTENSEN ET AL.
Methodological considerations
The sample size of the present study was based on a sample size predicting a need for 20
included participants. However, only 16 individuals completed this study hence the
findings of the present study might be prone to type two errors.
 Kicking accuracy was measured in kicks with a requirement of ≥ 80% individual
maximum kicking speed as kicking accuracy decreases as the speed requirement
increases (Andersen & Dörge, 2011; Hunter et al., 2018).
 The methodological approach resulted in the exclusion of kicks falling below this
threshold. We did not systematically analyse or count the excluded kicks in all partici­
pants. However, if the number of kicks below the speed-criterium is influenced, this
outcome may represent valuable additional information for future studies.
Perspectives and practical applications
The results from this study indicate that maximal kicking speed is reduced with muscle
fatigue and kicking distribution is altered with an increased error ellipse shorts axis.
A possible effect of this is a reduced chance on goal scoring on a given kick late in the
game when players experience muscle fatigue.
 A goalkeeper’s reach is determined by the speed of the kick when taken from the penalty
spot. A given goalkeeper’s maximal take-off velocity is constant, and the variable in the
situation is the time it takes for the ball to travel after being kicked from the kicker’s foot
determining the time for the goalkeeper to travel after taking off from the ground. The faster
the ball travels, the less time the goalkeeper can travel before the ball passes by and enters the
goal. On the intervention day during the accuracy measurements, the players kicked on
average 27.88 m/s ±1.16 m/s before fatigue and 27.44 m/s ±1.37 m/s after fatigue, providing
the goalkeeper with an additional 0.0064s (1.6%) to react to the kick. The increased reaction
time may extend the goalkeeper’s reach during the kick and hence reduces the chance of goal
scoring. The decrease in average ball speed during the accuracy test although not statistically
significant followed the decrease in maximal ball speed of 1.9% corresponding to equal effort
levels during the tests. On the control day average ball speed during the accuracy test did not
change statistically but increased numerically from 27,69 m/s ±1.21 m/s to 27.92 m/s ±1.09
m/s an increase of 0.8% following a similar small non-significant increase of 0.2% in the
maximal ball speed test again corresponding to equal effort levels during these tests.
 Furthermore, the increased error ellipse describing the dispersion pattern of kicks could
bring about changes in the proportion of kicks ending up in the ‘scoring zone’ (inside the
goal but outside the reach of the goalkeeper). The areas of the dispersion ellipses were not
significantly altered after fatigue in the present study. Therefore, the effect of muscle fatigue
would be the altered shape of the error ellipse. Depending on the aiming point this more
elongated error ellipse possibly results in a reduced number of shots ending up in the
‘scoring zone’ or alter the optimal point of aim more centrally in the goal.
Conclusion
The findings of the present study showed a reduction in the players’ maximum kicking
speed following a fatigue inducing protocol of the quadriceps femoris muscle. A decrease
  SPORTS BIOMECHANICS 17
in maximum foot speed immediately before ball contact is likely the cause of the lowered
maximum kicking speed. The effect on kicking accuracy is not conclusive due to greater
data variation and a lack of statistical power in the study. However, an improved kicking
accuracy was observed on the control day, but not on the day of the fatigue intervention.
The implications of muscle-fatiguing work on kicking skills are, however, not definitively
described in this study and require further research.

 "confidence":"medium",
 "studyDesign":"Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Mixed / General Sport"],
 "populations":["Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Randomised repeated-measures laboratory study of 25 healthy participants (10 women, 15 men) performing running, drop jumps and 180-degree change of direction barefoot, with fresh ankle tape, and after 15 minutes of sports-specific use, with 3D motion capture and force plates. Fresh tape significantly reduced peak ankle inversion, and most ACL and running overuse risk factors were unchanged or reduced. Peak loading rate of the ground reaction force increased by 4% to 18% between movements. Some effects remained after 15 minutes of use, while others moved closer to barefoot.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Participants were described as healthy adults with no recent injury, not as athletes, and the study tested biomechanics in a lab with barefoot movement rather than in sports footwear. Injury outcomes were not measured, and the authors state that the effects after longer use and in chronic ankle instability are unknown.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the reduced ankle inversion as proof that taping prevents sprains, when the study measured only biomechanical variables in healthy people and no injuries.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Utku B, Bähr G, Knoke H, Mai P, Paganini F, Hipper M, et al. The effect of fresh and used ankle taping on lower limb biomechanics in sports specific movements. Journal of Science and Medicine in Sport. 2024.",
   "doi":"10.1016/j.jsams.2024.07.002",
   "abstract":"Twenty-five healthy participants performed running, drop jumping and 180-degree change-of-direction movements barefoot, with fresh ankle tape, and after 15 minutes of sports-specific use. Kinetic and kinematic variables related to ankle sprain, ACL and overuse injury risk were measured using 3D motion capture and force platforms.",
   "tldr":"Fresh ankle taping reduced peak ankle inversion during running, jumping and change-of-direction movements in healthy adults. Most ACL and overuse risk measures did not rise, but peak loading rate did increase, and some effects were still present after 15 minutes of use.",
   "methods":"Randomised repeated-measures design with barefoot (BF), fresh tape (TF) and tape after 15 minutes of sports-specific use (TU) conditions, with sex as a between-subject factor. Twenty-five healthy participants (10 women, 15 men) performed drop jumps from 25 cm, running at 4.5 m/s and 180-degree change of direction at 3.0 m/s on a force platform, with three valid trials per movement and condition. Kinematics were recorded by 22 cameras at 200 Hz and kinetics by two force platforms at 1000 Hz. Standard taping was applied by one sports physician. Participants ran, accelerated, changed direction and jumped in their own sports shoes for 15 minutes between TF and TU data collection.",
   "findings":"Fresh tape and tape after sports-specific use significantly reduced peak ankle inversion. Most biomechanical risk factors for ACL or running overuse injury were unchanged or decreased with fresh tape, except peak loading rate of the resultant ground reaction force, which increased by 4% to 18% between movements. After 15 minutes of use, some effects of fresh tape remained, while others moved closer to barefoot values. Ankle dorsiflexion was significantly restricted by taping during change of direction and running, and the fresh-tape effect on some variables differed between women and men.",
   "limitations":"Participants were healthy and not athletes, and no athletes with chronic ankle instability were tested. Only one taping method was used, and the study was done in a lab with barefoot conditions, which the authors note does not reflect shod use in sport. Only 15 minutes of sports-specific use was tested, so the time course of protection is unknown. The study measured biomechanics only, not injuries.",
   "practicalImplications":"Fresh ankle taping can reduce peak ankle inversion during sports movements in healthy players, which is the mechanism linked to sprain risk. Taping did not clearly raise most ACL and running-overuse risk factors, but the higher loading rate means staff should watch for overuse symptoms. The effects after 15 minutes of use were mixed, so taping should not be assumed to protect equally throughout a session.",
   "athleteDev":"Taping may reduce ankle inversion during running, landing and cutting, with little change to most knee and hip risk measures. Staff should watch loading rate and overuse symptoms, since the ground reaction force loading rate increased.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot be used to set return-to-play decisions. It tested healthy participants with no injuries and did not include athletes with chronic ankle instability or recent sprains."
 }
}

 Conclusions: Ankle taping protects the ankle joint by reducing biomechanical risk factors associated with ankle

{
 "id":"Q58",
 "sourceFile":"The effect of body mass on eccentric knee-flexor   strength assessed with an instrumented Nordic hamstring   device-Nordbord-in football players.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The Effect of Body Mass on Eccentric Knee-Flexor Strength Assessed With an Instrumented Nordic Hamstring Device (Nordbord) in Football Players' (IJSPP 2016) matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cross-sectional Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Monitoring & Technology",
 "domains":["Monitoring & Technology","Sports Medicine & Injury"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Athletic Training","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Soccer","Other Sport"],
 "populations":["Youth / Adolescent","Professional / Elite","Healthy Athletes"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Cross-sectional analysis of single-visit Nordbord eccentric knee-flexor testing in 122 football players: 81 soccer players (U17, U19, U21 academy, 4th French division, and professional) and 41 Australian Football League players, all tested in season. Eccentric strength correlated largely with body mass (r = 0.55, 90% CI 0.42 to 0.64) and was not materially changed by adjustment for body fat. The authors report the regression equation eccentric strength (N) = 4 x body mass (kg) + 26.1, and that only the professional soccer players were likely slightly (about 20%) stronger than their body-mass-expected values.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Data were collected as routine in-season monitoring in six squads, with one test visit per player and no injury outcomes, so the equation describes strength differences but cannot show that body-mass adjustment predicts injury risk. Sex is not stated explicitly in the text, and the regression is specific to these groups.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the body-mass equation as a validated injury threshold, when the study only quantifies how test scores vary with body mass and gives no injury data.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2016,
   "citation":"Buchheit M, Cholley Y, Nagel M, Poulos N. The Effect of Body Mass on Eccentric Knee-Flexor Strength Assessed With an Instrumented Nordic Hamstring Device (Nordbord) in Football Players. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2016;11(6):721-726.",
   "doi":"10.1123/ijspp.2015-0513",
   "abstract":"Data from 81 soccer players (youth academy, 4th French division and professional) and 41 AFL players were used to examine how body mass affects eccentric knee-flexor strength measured with the Nordbord. Eccentric strength correlated largely with body mass, and the authors offer a regression equation to compare individual test results with body-mass-expected values.",
   "tldr":"Nordbord eccentric hamstring strength rises with body mass, so a single absolute threshold may misclassify heavier and lighter players. Practitioners can compare an athlete's score with the body-mass-expected value from the reported equation.",
   "methods":"Single-visit Nordbord testing (one set of three maximal Nordic hamstring repetitions, average of both legs) in 122 players from six groups, collected in season as routine monitoring. Body mass, skinfolds and percentage body fat were measured. Linear regression, log-transformed data, allometric scaling and magnitude-based inference were used. Players with an injury in the prior six months were excluded.",
   "findings":"Across all players, eccentric knee-flexor strength correlated largely with body mass (r = 0.55, 90% CI 0.42 to 0.64); adjusting for body fat did not change the correlation. The regression equation is eccentric strength (N) = 4 x body mass (kg) + 26.1, with a typical error of about 22% (65 N). Absolute strength was highest in the professional soccer group (411 +/- 65 N), and only the professional soccer players were likely slightly (about 20%) stronger than their body-mass-expected values.",
   "limitations":"This was a cross-sectional analysis of one test visit per player, so it cannot show test-retest change or injury prediction. Data came from six groups with different ages, standards and training histories, and the allometric exponent varied between them (0.57 to 1.51). Sex is not stated explicitly in the text. Individual differences smaller than about 40 N (12%) could not be reliably judged in a single test.",
   "practicalImplications":"When comparing players of different body mass, or tracking one player whose body mass changes, staff can compare the Nordbord score with the body-mass-expected value from the reported equation. A single absolute strength threshold without body-mass adjustment may be misleading. The study gives no data on whether the adjusted values predict injury.",
   "athleteDev":"Use the body-mass-expected Nordbord value to judge whether an individual's eccentric knee-flexor strength is below or above expectation. Differences under about 40 N (12%) in a single test should not be read as meaningful.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot be used to judge return to sport or set clearance criteria. It contains no injured-player or post-injury data, and it excludes players with recent injury."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "athleteDev: removed unsupported advice 'Regular retesting would give stronger evidence of change' (not stated in the paper)",
     "populations: added Healthy Athletes ('Data from players with an injury sustained within the 6 months preceding the study were not included')",
     "screeningLimitations/limitations: 'Sex is not stated' -> 'not stated explicitly' (players are referred to as 'his' but sex is never reported)"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"",
   "spotCheckPriority":"normal"
 }
}

 "audiences":["Performance","Nutrition","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Combat Sports"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Double-blind, counterbalanced, randomised crossover study of 14 highly trained male judo athletes at international level (20 were screened). Four sessions, at least one week apart: placebo with no nap, a 20-minute nap with placebo, 5 mg/kg caffeine without a nap, and caffeine plus a 20-minute nap, followed by a running-based anaerobic sprint test. Compared with placebo, all treatments increased maximum and mean sprint power, and caffeine (with or without a nap) increased minimum power; post-exercise creatine kinase and urea were higher with caffeine, and superoxide dismutase was higher after napping (glutathione peroxidase did not differ from placebo in the table).",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only 14 male athletes, all caffeine-naive and non-habitual nappers, were tested in a laboratory repeated-sprint protocol that the authors say does not reflect field conditions. The study used one caffeine dose and a single 20-minute nap, and the authors caution that results may not carry over to regular caffeine users or female athletes.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could treat caffeine plus a short nap as a proven pre-session strategy for any athlete, when the sample was 14 well-rested, caffeine-naive male judokas and caffeine also raised post-exercise muscle-damage markers.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Romdhani M, Souissi N, Dergaa I, Moussa-Chamari I, Chaabouni Y, Mahdouani K, et al. The effect of caffeine, nap opportunity and their combination on biomarkers of muscle damage and antioxidant defence during repeated sprint exercise. Biology of Sport. 2022;39(4):1033-1042.",
   "doi":"10.5114/biolsport.2023.112088",
   "abstract":"Fourteen highly trained male judo athletes completed four randomised, double-blind sessions: placebo with no nap, a 20-minute nap with placebo, 5 mg/kg caffeine, and caffeine plus a 20-minute nap. Repeated sprint power, plasma energy and muscle-damage markers, and antioxidant enzymes were measured around a running-based anaerobic sprint test.",
   "tldr":"A moderate caffeine dose (5 mg/kg) improved minimum sprint power and repeated sprint performance after a normal night's sleep, more than a 20-minute nap did. Caffeine also raised muscle-damage markers, while napping raised superoxide dismutase activity.",

{
 "id":"Q60",
 "sourceFile":"The effect of cam and pincer morphology on hamstring injury rates and return to play in elite young male football players.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The Effect of cam and pincer morphology on hamstring injury rates and return to play in elite young male football players' (Acta Orthop Traumatol Turc 2023) matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Cohort Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Sports Medicine & Injury",
 "domains":["Sports Medicine & Injury","Rehabilitation & Return to Sport"],
 "audiences":["Sports Medicine","Rehabilitation","Athletic Training"],
 "sports":["Soccer"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Youth / Adolescent","Professional / Elite"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Prognostic cohort study of 75 elite young male football academy players from one Turkish Super League club, with radiological screening for cam and pincer morphology at pre-season or pre-transfer examinations and six seasons of injury data. Players with cam and/or pincer morphology (n = 23) had a higher hamstring injury rate than players without (14/23, 60.9% vs 18/52, 34.6%; p = 0.034). Recurrence (35.7% vs 27.8%, p = 0.631) and treatment duration (18.4 +/- 10.1 vs 12.1 +/- 6.2 days) were higher in the morphology group, but these differences were not statistically significant.",
 "screeningLimitations":"The morphology group was small (n = 23), and the two groups differed in age and body weight. Morphology was not separated into cam, pincer and mixed types, and the study has no kinematic or range-of-motion data, so it cannot show the mechanism.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the association as proof that cam and pincer morphology causes hamstring injury, when the study is a small single-club observational comparison with a significant unadjusted difference in injury rate.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2023,
   "citation":"Dinç E, Arslan S, Akıkol M. The effect of cam and pincer morphology on hamstring injury rates and return to play in elite young male football players. Acta Orthop Traumatol Turc. 2023;57(1):36-39.",
   "doi":"10.5152/j.aott.2023.22115",
   "abstract":"Seventy-five elite young male football academy players were screened radiologically for femoroacetabular impingement and followed for six seasons. Players with cam and/or pincer morphology (n = 23) were compared with those without (n = 52) for hamstring injury count, recurrence and treatment duration.",
   "tldr":"In one elite academy, young male football players with cam or pincer hip morphology had a higher rate of hamstring injury than players without it. Recurrence and time to return were higher too, but these differences were not statistically significant.",
   "methods":"Prospective data collection with retrospective analysis over six seasons in 75 elite young male academy players from one club. Hip morphology was assessed on pelvic radiographs at pre-season or pre-transfer examinations using alpha angle, lateral centre-edge angle and Tonnis angle criteria. Non-contact hamstring injuries, their treatment durations and recurrences were recorded. Chi-square and independent-samples t-tests were used, with P < 0.05 as significant.",
   "findings":"The hamstring injury rate was higher in players with cam and/or pincer morphology (14 of 23, 60.9%) than without (18 of 52, 34.6%; p = 0.034). Recurrence was 35.7% (5 of 14) vs 27.8% (5 of 18), p = 0.631. Treatment duration was 18.4 +/- 10.1 days vs 12.1 +/- 6.2 days, which was not significant. Morphology players were older (20.35 vs 18.92 years) and heavier (71.5 vs 67.7 kg), and these differences were significant.",
   "limitations":"The morphology group was small (n = 23) and the two groups differed in age and body weight, which were not adjusted for. Cam, pincer and mixed morphologies were grouped together, and the sample was one male academy in one country. Range of motion and muscle-length data were not collected. The Results text gives 60.09% and the Highlights 60.1% for injury in the morphology group, but 14 of 23 is 60.9%, which matches Table 2. No p-value is reported for the treatment duration comparison, and the printed inclusion criteria (including a hamstring injury diagnosis within 1 year of the radiograph) are hard to reconcile with the uninjured players in the sample.",
   "practicalImplications":"Screening for cam and pincer morphology could help identify young football players who may have a higher hamstring injury rate, so staff may want to monitor them more closely. The study does not show that morphology causes injury or that it changes recovery time. Hip morphology alone should not be used to decide training load or playing availability.",
   "athleteDev":"Young players with cam or pincer morphology may warrant closer hamstring monitoring and prevention work. This is an association from one academy, so it should guide monitoring rather than set training prescriptions.",
   "rtp":"The study reports time to return after hamstring injury, but the difference was not significant and the sample was small. It cannot set return-to-play criteria or show that morphology should change clearance timing."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "limitations: replaced unclear sentence 'Figure 1 treatment durations are not significant' with 'No p-value is reported for the treatment duration comparison' (text only says 'statistically the results were not significant (Figure 1)')",
     "limitations: added Highlights value ('60.1% vs 34.6%') to the reported percentage inconsistency and noted the confusing inclusion criteria ('being diagnosed with a non-contact HMI within 1 year of the radiograph ... were determined as inclusion criteria')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"",
   "spotCheckPriority":"normal"
 }
}

 "id":"Q62",
 "sourceFile":"The effect of exercise-induced fatigue and heat exposure on soccer-specific decision-making during high intensity intermittent exercise.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The effect of exercise-induced fatigue and heat exposure on soccer-specific decision-making during high-intensity intermittent exercise' (PLOS ONE 2022) matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Laboratory / Experimental Study",
 "primaryDomain":"Brain Health & Psychology",
 "domains":["Brain Health & Psychology","Training & Performance"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Soccer"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Laboratory study of nine well-trained male university soccer players who completed a 92-minute cycling intermittent sprint protocol at 32 C (hot) and 18 C (temperate), responding to soccer-specific decision-making trials during the protocol. Decision-making scores were lower in the heat (86.87 +/- 7.95% vs 92.49 +/- 3.13%, p = 0.030), with no condition by time interaction. Peak power fell from the first to the second half only in the heat, although it did not differ between conditions within either half, and plasma normetanephrine and metanephrine rose more in the heat. Ten players were planned, but testing stopped early because of the pandemic, so trial order was not fully counterbalanced.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only nine players were analysed, the trial order was only partly counterbalanced, and the protocol used cycling rather than running. The decision-making task was a single visual task, and with no interaction effect the lower scores in heat cannot be attributed to fatigue during exercise rather than to heat exposure itself.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the lower decision-making scores as a clear hot-weather effect on match decision-making, when the interaction was not significant and the sample was nine players in a cycling-based protocol.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2022,
   "citation":"Donnan KJ, Williams EL, Stanger N. The effect of exercise-induced fatigue and heat exposure on soccer-specific decision-making during high-intensity intermittent exercise. PLoS ONE. 2022;17(12):e0279109.",
   "doi":"10.1371/journal.pone.0279109",
   "abstract":"Nine well-trained male soccer players completed a 92-minute cycling intermittent sprint protocol at 32 C (hot) and 18 C (temperate), responding to soccer-specific decision-making trials throughout. Physical output, decision-making, appraisal, affect and plasma metanephrines were measured.",
   "tldr":"In nine trained soccer players, heat lowered soccer-specific decision-making during a prolonged intermittent sprint protocol. Power output also fell in the second half only in the heat, with a more threatening appraisal and higher stress hormone levels.",
   "methods":"Laboratory study with nine well-trained male soccer players, planned as a counterbalanced design for 10 players but stopped early because of the pandemic (five players began in 32 C, four in 18 C). Participants completed a 92-minute cycling intermittent sprint protocol (5-s sprints against 8% body mass with active recovery at 35% of the VO2peak from an incremental test) at 32 C and 50% relative humidity or 18 C and 50% relative humidity. Soccer-specific decision-making was scored against expert panel responses and verbal think-aloud reports were coded. Analysis used two-way repeated-measures ANOVA and content analysis.",
   "findings":"Decision-making scores were lower in 32 C than 18 C (86.87 +/- 7.95% vs 92.49 +/- 3.13%, main effect p = 0.030), but there was no condition by time interaction. Peak power fell in the second half of the protocol only in the heat (about 7%), with no significant between-condition difference in either half. Plasma normetanephrine was higher in the heat at half-time (p = 0.012) and post-exercise (p < 0.001), and metanephrine was higher post-exercise (p = 0.006 to 0.009). Players verbalised less future planning in the heat (p = 0.030, d = 0.20), and threat appraisal and unpleasant affect were higher in the heat (p = 0.007 and p = 0.008).",
   "limitations":"Only nine players were analysed, and the planned 10 were not reached. Trial order was only partly counterbalanced. A cycling protocol was used, which the authors say may produce less physiological strain than running. The decision-making task was visual only and did not reproduce dual-task demands of match play. Decision-making was lower in the heat at all time points, including pre-exercise in the chamber, so passive heat exposure may explain part of the effect. Laboratory motivation may differ from matches. The think-aloud findings need caution given the number of analyses run. Core temperature averaged about 38.4 C in the heat, with no main condition effect, and the authors say this is lower than typical team-sport values.",
   "practicalImplications":"In hot conditions, soccer players may make poorer decisions and lose work output, even when core temperature stays below common cut-offs. Staff planning training or matches in heat should consider decision-making as well as physical output. Players also reported more threat and unpleasant feelings in the heat, and the authors suggest strategies such as acclimatisation or re-appraisal could be considered.",
   "athleteDev":"Heat can lower decision-making and second-half work output during intermittent exercise, even when core temperature stays around 38.4 C. Staff should consider cognitive as well as physical demands when preparing players for hot conditions.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot be used for return-to-play decisions. It tested healthy trained players in a laboratory cycling protocol and includes no injury or rehabilitation outcomes."
 },

   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "methods: 'high-intensity workload set from their own VO2max test' -> sprints 'against a resistance of 8% body mass' with '105-s of active recovery at 35% VO2peak'",
