     "limitations/screeningLimitations: added that decision-making was lower in heat at all time points including rest ('Decision-making score was found to be lower throughout all time-points ... passive exposure to hot conditions may have contributed')",
     "findings: added small effect size for future planning ('d = 0.20'); metanephrine p-value range reflects text (p = .006) and abstract (p = .009)",
     "practicalImplications/athleteDev: replaced generic coaching advice with the authors' suggested strategies ('acclimatisation, cognitive or emotional-regulation strategies such as re-appraisal')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"",
   "spotCheckPriority":"normal"
 }
}

{
 "id":"Q63",
 "sourceFile":"The effect of fatiguing muscle contractions on kicking performance in experienced soccer players.pdf",
 "decision":"INCLUDE",
 "exclusionReason":"",
 "degradedReason":"",
 "doiMissing":false,
 "identityCheck":"Title in text 'The effect of fatiguing muscle contractions on kicking performance in experienced soccer players' (Sports Biomechanics, Carstensen et al.) matches the filename.",
 "confidence":"high",
 "studyDesign":"Randomized Controlled Trial",
 "primaryDomain":"Training & Performance",
 "domains":["Training & Performance","Recovery & Readiness"],
 "audiences":["Performance","Coaching","Research & Analytics"],
 "sports":["Soccer"],
 "populations":["Male Athletes","Mixed / Unspecified"],
 "evidenceSummary":"Randomised crossover study of 16 male soccer players (5 professional, 11 amateur; 17 recruited, one dropout) who completed a fatiguing protocol (5 sets of 10 maximal concentric and eccentric knee extensions) and a rest control on separate days, with kicking tests before and after. The protocol reduced maximal voluntary isometric contraction force by 14.0 +/- 2.7%. Maximum ball speed fell 1.9% after fatigue, and the change was 2.1% greater than control. Shooting accuracy did not differ significantly between conditions (p = 0.18); accuracy improved on the control day and did not change after fatigue.",
 "screeningLimitations":"Only 16 players were analysed, the authors say the study lacks statistical power for accuracy (calculated power 65%), and the protocol was a single knee-extension fatigue model rather than match-type fatigue. Ball and foot speed came from each player's hardest kick only.",
 "synthesisCaution":"Staff could read the small ball-speed decline as a match-relevant loss of shooting performance, when the accuracy effect was not significant and the control-day improvement was unexpected.",
 "paper":{
   "year":2024,
   "citation":"Carstensen JB, Gaemelke T, Overgaard K, Andersen TB. The effect of fatiguing muscle contractions on kicking performance in experienced soccer players. Sports Biomechanics. 2024.",
   "doi":"10.1080/14763141.2024.2433084",
   "abstract":"Sixteen male soccer players (5 professional, 11 amateur) completed kicking tests after a fatiguing quadriceps protocol or rest, on separate days in a randomised crossover design. Maximal voluntary isometric contraction force, stimulation force ratio and kicking speed and accuracy were measured before and after each condition.",
   "tldr":"Fatiguing the quadriceps lowered maximal kicking ball speed in experienced soccer players. Shooting accuracy did not change significantly, although the study was too small to rule out an effect.",
   "methods":"Randomised crossover with 16 analysed male players (17 recruited, one dropout) from amateur to professional level, aged 18 to 30 years with at least 10 years of organised play. On separate days, participants completed a fatiguing protocol (5 sets of 10 maximal voluntary concentric and eccentric knee extensions with the kicking leg) or a rest control. Maximal isometric force, the 15 Hz/50 Hz stimulation force ratio, maximum ball speed, foot speed and shooting accuracy were measured before and after. Paired t-tests and repeated-measures ANOVA with Bonferroni correction were used.",
   "findings":"The fatiguing protocol reduced maximal isometric force by 14.0 +/- 2.7% and the force ratio by 14.0 +/- 3.7%, with no reduction in control. Maximum ball speed fell 1.9% after fatigue (0.57 m/s), with no change on the control day, and the change differed significantly between conditions (2.1%). Maximum foot speed fell 5.87% after fatigue, but the between-day difference was not significant (p = 0.054). Shooting accuracy improved 13.3% on the control day (p = 0.02) but did not change on the fatigue day, and the between-condition difference was not significant (p = 0.18). The short axis of the kick dispersion ellipse widened by 53.9% after fatigue, significantly more than on the control day.",
   "limitations":"Only 16 players were analysed, and the authors state there was insufficient power for the accuracy outcome. The control-day accuracy improvement was unexpected by the authors and shows why a control condition matters when judging fatigue effects. Ball and foot speed were taken from each player's hardest kick, and accuracy kicks below 80% of maximum speed were discarded without being counted. Fatigue was induced in one muscle group with knee extensions, not match conditions. The ball-speed effect was small, at about 2%.",
   "practicalImplications":"Heavy quadriceps work can reduce maximum kicking speed in trained players for at least the 30 minutes or so of testing that followed. The study found no clear effect on accuracy, so it does not show that fatigue harms shot placement. Practitioners should not assume a shooting-accuracy loss from this evidence.",
   "athleteDev":"Fatiguing quadriceps work lowered maximum kick speed by about 2% in this group, but accuracy was not clearly affected. The study did not test how to sequence strength work and shooting practice.",
   "rtp":"This study cannot be used for return-to-play decisions. It tested healthy players with an induced quadriceps fatigue protocol and included no injury or rehabilitation outcomes."
 },
 "verification":{
   "status":"CORRECTED",
   "changes":[
     "findings: added non-significant between-day foot speed difference ('6.30%, CI = [-0.001%; 12,7%], p = 0.054') and the dispersion ellipse result ('short axis increased by 53.9% ... increased significantly more on the intervention day')",
     "limitations: replaced garbled 'may reflect learning or a lack of control in other studies' with the authors' point ('comes as a surprise to us ... demonstrating the importance of including a control group'); clarified the hardest-kick and 80%-speed exclusion rules ('We did not systematically analyse or count the excluded kicks')",
     "practicalImplications/athleteDev: removed unsupported advice on separating lower-limb work and skill practice; the study did not test sequencing",
     "methods: added paired t-tests ('The results were compared using paired t-tests')"
   ],
   "residualConcerns":"Year 2024 is the online-first year ('Published online: 04 Dec 2024'); no journal volume, issue or pages are printed, so check whether the batch lead wants online-first records coded DEGRADED.",
   "spotCheckPriority":"high"
 }
}
